detail.abstract: As artificial superintelligence (ASI) becomes more technically viable, the risk of an arms race between the United States and China increases. This paper proposes a phased, enforceable treaty designed to reduce that risk by using mutual vulnerability to align incentives. Drawing on lessons from nuclear arms control, the treaty includes verifiable limits on compute and model training, telemetry-based inspections, and bilateral emergency protocols. Unlike frameworks based on voluntary norms, this model integrates oversight into national security infrastructure, making coordination possible even without trust. It addresses near-term safety risks and long-term shifts in global power, offering a strategy that reflects current geopolitical conditions. The treaty is built to function under rivalry, not consensus, and includes mechanisms for adaptability in the face of political change or external disruption. While focused on the U.S. and China, the structure could support future multilateral expansion as other actors approach ASI capabilities.

title: Users Prefer Generative AI to Depict What is Real Instead of What is Ideal
affiliations: , University of Hohenheim - Faculty of Business, Economics and Social Sciences and University of Hohenheim

detail.title: Users Prefer Generative AI to Depict What is Real Instead of What is Ideal
detail.abstract: The representation of social categories by generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is often considered biased and thus unfair. But there exist several mutually exclusive ethical standards according to which a bias can be established. While different authors seem to take different standards for granted, users’ consideration of what constitutes an appropriate representation is rarely elicited. However, if we want to keep humans in the loop of decision-making, we should make sure that artificial intelligence (AI) does not nudge them away from what they deem morally relevant upon reflection. Our study, therefore, investigates users’ evaluations of the appropriate representation of gender proportions in various social categories. We find that the much discussed standards of uniform equality and substantive equality play little role in these evaluations. Users desire a representation that reflects their perception of reality. Our results suggest that user-centric  GAI should rely on empirical data when representing gender in social categories.

title: Digital Fragmentation as a Contemporary Trend in the Global Economy

detail.title: Digital Fragmentation as a Contemporary Trend in the Global Economy
detail.abstract: Digital fragmentation is an increasingly defining and complex trend in the global economy of the 21st century. This process refers to the progressive stratification of the digital sphere, driven by the convergence of technological competition, divergent regulatory regimes, and geopolitical strategies. Fragmentation manifests across multiple, interconnected dimensions: at the technological level through competing, incompatible platforms and ecosystems in areas like cloud computing and IoT; at the regulatory level via disparate national frameworks for data governance, cybersecurity, and digital taxation; and at the geopolitical level through policies aimed at technological sovereignty and protectionism, leading to the emergence of distinct digital domains centered around major powers or blocs like the US, China, and the EU. The economic implications of this trend are profoundly ambivalent. While it may foster regional innovation hubs and enhance data security, it simultaneously imposes significant costs on international businesses through heightened transaction expenses, market adaptation burdens, and increased supply chain complexity. Consequently, digital fragmentation is reshaping the fundamental architecture of the global economic system. Its future trajectory will depend on the evolving balance between competing forces—market dynamics, state intervention, and international governance—as they seek to reconcile the imperatives of openness, security, competition, and cooperation. Understanding this phenomenon necessitates a comprehensive, interdisciplinary approach that integrates insights from economics, political science, and technology studies.

title: Sustainability-Linked Debt, Capital Structure, and Endogenous Default
affiliations: Ulm University - Institute of Insurance Science and Ulm University - Institute of Insurance Science

detail.title: Sustainability-Linked Debt, Capital Structure, and Endogenous Default
detail.abstract: We develop a structural credit model of perpetual debt financing in which firms issue sustainability-linked bonds (SLBs) whose coupons step up via penalty payments when predefined sustainability targets are missed. Focusing on firms that aim to reduce emissions, we show that SLBs operate through two distinct channels: the firm can choose a lower endogenous bankruptcy threshold while holding equity value constant, or it can attain a significantly higher total firm value. In the first channel—when the bankruptcy threshold is set lower—SLBs reshape default incentives, extend expected firm lifetime, and can raise debt capacity without proportionally increasing distress costs. As a supplementary extension, we incorporate carbon taxes and subsidies to reflect policy-driven effects on cash flows and incentives, without changing the central mechanism through which SLBs affect default and leverage choices.

title: Tidal Power, Energy Security, and Decarbonization

detail.title: Tidal Power, Energy Security, and Decarbonization
detail.abstract: This paper assesses whether large-scale tidal energy can contribute to energy security and decarbonization by reducing fossil fuel dependence and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions intensity. Focusing on South Korea, we exploit the full operationalization of the Sihwa Lake Tidal Power Station in 2012 as a natural experiment. Using national time-series analysis, difference-in-differences estimations against Japan and a broader group of Asia–Pacific economies, and a synthetic control approach, the study examines changes in energy intensity, electricity generation by fuel type, and per-capita CO2 emissions. The synthetic control method constructs a data-driven counterfactual for South Korea based on comparable Asia–Pacific economies, providing a transparent benchmark for assessing post-treatment deviations in coal-based electricity generation and coal-related emissions. Across all empirical strategies, the results consistently indicate that sustained tidal energy deployment is associated with a significant decline in overall energy intensity and a marked reduction in coal-based electricity generation. Correspondingly, per-capita CO2 emissions from coal and coal's relative contribution to total emissions fall significantly, while aggregate per-capita emissions remain broadly stable. Pre-trend tests and the close pre-treatment fit of the synthetic control support the validity of the identification strategy. The estimated effects persist after controlling for international climate policy through a Paris Agreement indicator, suggesting that tidal energy contributes independently to structural changes in the energy system. Overall, the findings provide rare long-run empirical evidence that large-scale tidal power can enhance energy security and support decarbonization primarily through the targeted displacement of coal.

detail.title: THE NCAA'S GAMBLING PROBLEM

publicationDetails.detailsText: U Iowa Legal Studies Research Paper Forthcoming

detail.abstract:
As legalization of, and participation in, sports gambling has increased, many United States professional sports leagues and teams have embraced it. While a new and lavish revenue source for these professional sports organizations, sports gambling has also had negative effects. Disgruntled bettors threaten and harass athletes and authorities have caught players participating in illicit wagering activity or influencing game outcomes for gamblers, the latter calling into question the sanctity of competition integrity.

At the same time, the primary governing body for college athletics – the NCAA – has not embraced sports gambling. In fact, NCAA rules go so far as to prohibit collegiate athletes, coaches, and athletics administrators from wagering on professional sporting events like the Super Bowl. Yet the NCAA and its member universities have had to endure the same negative effects of sports gambling like bettors harassing athletes and athletes’ involvement in gambling without benefitting from the influx of significant revenue like many professional sports organizations.

The NCAA’s 2025 dalliance with a potential rule change that would have permitted collegiate athletes, coaches, and athletics administrators to bet on professional sports exemplifies the NCAA’s struggle with sports gambling. While the NCAA implemented the rule change, its member universities quickly overrode it.

This Article explores the NCAA’s complicated relationship with legalized sports gambling, including its recent near rule change. Specifically, the Article examines whether and how the rule’s adoption would have decreased the number of NCAA rules enforcement actions at a time when proliferation of sports gambling concerns many from an addiction standpoint and collegiate athletes have access to increased income through both name, image, and likeness and revenue share compensation. The Article also proposes ways the NCAA can combat both gambling-related harassment and athletes’ involvement in activities that mitigate game integrity and suggests ways athletics administrators can protect their university in the event of their athletes’ involvement in illicit sports gambling.

detail.abstract: The rapid digitalization of organizational processes has significantly increased exposure to cybersecurity risks, making effective risk assessment and audit frameworks critical for organizational resilience. Cyber incidents not only disrupt operations but also undermine stakeholder trust, regulatory compliance, and corporate governance structures. This study examines existing cybersecurity risk assessment and audit frameworks, focusing on their effectiveness in supporting regulatory compliance and strengthening governance mechanisms. Drawing on established standards such as ISO/IEC 27001, NIST Cybersecurity Framework, COBIT, and SOC reporting, the paper evaluates how organizations integrate cybersecurity audits into enterprise risk management and governance systems. Using a conceptual and analytical approach supported by secondary data, regulatory guidance, and prior empirical studies, this research identifies gaps between compliance-driven audits and risk-based cybersecurity governance. The findings highlight the need for continuous, integrated, and governance-oriented cybersecurity auditing models that go beyond checklist compliance. The study contributes to the literature by proposing an integrated cybersecurity risk assessment and audit framework aligned with corporate governance objectives, regulatory expectations, and strategic risk management.

title: Sibling Sex Composition and Marriage Outcomes
affiliations: , University of California and University of California, Merced

detail.title: Sibling Sex Composition and Marriage Outcomes
detail.abstract: Marriage patterns vary substantially across U.S. populations, yet family dynamics influencing these differentials remain understudied. We examine how sibling sex composition affects marriage timing and prevalence using vital statistics covering all 6.6 million births in Texas from 1976-1997 linked to marriage and divorce records through 2019. Results show that first-born individuals with same-sex younger siblings marry at rates 6.3% higher and approximately one month earlier than those with opposite-sex siblings. Twin comparisons, which eliminate birth order effects, reveal effects twice as large. However, substantial demographic heterogeneity emerges: associations concentrate almost entirely among non-Hispanic Whites and in higher-income counties, with minimal or opposite patterns for Black and Hispanic populations. These findings illuminate how family structure operates differently across cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds, contributing to understanding of demographic stratification in contemporary U.S. marriage patterns.

detail.title: Nonparametric Estimation and Testing of Heterogeneous Nonlinear Temperature-Yield Relationships
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a mixed sieve-kernel estimator for the nonlinear crop yield response model of Schlenker and Roberts (2009). Annual crop yields are modeled as the integral of an unknown yield response function with respect to a within-season temperature density, which is estimated nonparametrically. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator in a panel data framework and develop a formal test for the equality of state-specific yield response functions. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate good finitesample performance. An empirical application to U.S. county-level corn yields from 1950 to 2020 replicates the well-documented nonlinear temperature-yield relationship and strongly rejects yield homogeneity across states, providing clear evidence of substantial spatial heterogeneity in climate sensitivity.

detail.abstract: Entrepreneurship and innovation play a central role in driving economic growth, employment generation, and structural transformation in emerging economies. Unlike developed markets, entrepreneurial activity in emerging economies occurs within environments characterized by institutional voids, financial constraints, regulatory uncertainty, and infrastructural deficiencies. At the same time, these contexts present unique opportunities for innovation, particularly frugal innovation, digital entrepreneurship, and inclusive business models that address unmet social and economic needs. This paper provides a comprehensive examination of the relationship between entrepreneurship and innovation in emerging economies. Drawing on existing theoretical frameworks and empirical literature, the study explores key drivers, constraints, and outcomes of entrepreneurial innovation in developing contexts. The paper further analyzes the role of institutions, technology adoption, access to finance, and government policy in shaping entrepreneurial ecosystems. By synthesizing prior research and proposing an integrative conceptual framework, this study contributes to the literature by highlighting context-specific mechanisms through which entrepreneurship fosters innovation-led development in emerging economies. Policy implications and directions for future research are also discussed.

detail.abstract: This Article extends the voluntary compliance framework developed in Can the Public Be Trusted? The Promise and Perils of Voluntary Compliance to the corporate context. While recent scholarship has explored when states can rely on non-coercive regulatory approaches with individual citizens, comparatively little attention has been paid to whether these insights translate to business entities. This Article argues that corporations present both greater challenges and greater opportunities for voluntary compliance regimes. On one hand, the instrumental orientation of corporate decision-making, amplified by fiduciary duties and competitive pressures, may systematically undermine the intrinsic motivations that voluntary compliance frameworks depend upon. Drawing on behavioral ethics research demonstrating that organizational settings can serve as "hotbeds for unethicality," this Article identifies structural features of corporate environments that impede genuine voluntary compliance. On the other hand, corporations possess characteristics that may actually facilitate trust-based regulation: they are repeat players sensitive to reputational consequences, they operate through transparent bureaucratic processes amenable to monitoring, and they cannot claim violations of personal autonomy when past behavior informs regulatory treatment. This Article synthesizes these competing considerations into a differentiated framework for corporate regulation, identifying the conditions under which non-coercive approaches are most likely to succeed across securities regulation, environmental compliance, and corporate governance more broadly.

title: Housing Beyond Reach? Evidence from Civil Servant Salaries in Greater Accra, Ghana

detail.title: Housing Beyond Reach? Evidence from Civil Servant Salaries in Greater Accra, Ghana
detail.abstract: Despite steady employment, many public sector workers in rapidly urbanising African cities face severe barriers to homeownership. This paper makes an important contribution to the ongoing research on housing affordability within developing economies. It critically examines purchase and mortgage affordability among essential civil service professionals in Ghana to assess their capacity for homeownership. The results demonstrate that housing remains profoundly unaffordable for key civil sector workers across most suburbs in the Greater Accra region. Even if all their income were dedicated exclusively to housing expenses, it would require approximately forty years to purchase a small, one-to-three-bedroom house, and around a hundred years for larger residences with four or more bedrooms. Furthermore, although certain Ghanaian financial institutions offer mortgage products, these workers would not meet the qualification criteria based solely on their salaries. Consequently, market housing, particularly listings available online, is effectively beyond their reach. The research concludes that, when considering only salary levels, housing affordability issues persist for prominent public sector employees such as immigration officers, nurses, police officers, and teachers. The substantial disparity between rental costs and ownership expenses indicates an urgent need for governmental intervention through targeted affordable housing initiatives.

title: Institutions, Commodity Rents, and Development Outcomes: Evidence from Ghana and Chile

detail.title: Institutions, Commodity Rents, and Development Outcomes: Evidence from Ghana and Chile
detail.abstract: Motivation: Commodity-exporting economies face persistent challenges in translating resource rents into stable and inclusive development outcomes. While commodity revenues can support public investment and macroeconomic stability, volatility and weak institutional coordination often undermine these potential benefits. Understanding how institutional arrangements mediate the impact of commodity rents remains central to development policy debates. Purpose: This article examines how institutional arrangements shape the development impact of commodity rents through a comparative analysis of Ghana and Chile. It asks how differences in fiscal coordination, rent management, and policy sequencing help explain divergent outcomes among commodity exporters facing similar external conditions. Approach and methods: The study adopts a qualitative comparative case study approach. It analyses policy frameworks, fiscal institutions, and sectoral linkages in Ghana and Chile, drawing on secondary sources and institutional evidence. The analysis is structured around a three-layer framework linking commodity rents, institutional mediation, and development outcomes. Findings: The findings show that differences in development outcomes are not primarily driven by the size of commodity rents, but by the quality of institutional coordination. Ghana's experience is characterised by fragmented rent management, limited absorptive capacity, and pro-cyclical spending. Chile, by contrast, has developed stabilisation mechanisms and coordination frameworks that insulate public spending from price volatility and facilitate spillovers. Policy implications: The analysis suggests that effective rent management must precede diversification strategies, that fiscal rules matter more than ownership structures, and that institutional sequencing must reflect country-specific constraints. These lessons are particularly relevant for late commodity producers seeking to manage volatility while supporting long-term development.

title: The Influence of Common Institutional Ownership on Corporate Tax Planning

detail.title: The Influence of Common Institutional Ownership on Corporate Tax Planning
detail.abstract: Common ownership has increased substantially over the past few decades and has become a significant influence on corporate policies. We find that firms owned by the same institution engage in more tax planning. We also observe that the influence of common ownership on corporate tax planning is stronger when the threat of sale is more credible. Further tests show that commonly owned firms exhibit less aggressive income tax reporting and more sustainable corporate tax outcomes. Finally, we revisit inferences from prior literature examining the effect of institutional ownership on tax planning and demonstrate that the magnitudes documented in previous research are strongest when a common owner is present. This latter result underscores the importance of considering the effect of common ownership on corporate tax policies.

detail.abstract: This chapter examines factors influencing graduate start-ups performance. It is grounded on the theories of organisational learning and social capital. Employing a sample of 156 graduate startups based in China, the study investigates the effect of knowledge strategies (exploration or exploitation) on graduate start-up performance, and the effects of social capital (structural, relational, and cognitive dimensions) on the deployment of knowledge strategies. The results indicate that strategic simplicity through the approach of knowledge exploitation could achieve better outcomes for graduate start-ups in the early stage of venture creation, that adaptive knowledge strategies are of crucial importance in sustaining new venture performance, and that graduate entrepreneurs need to approach networking strategically in order to cultivate social capital, particularly trust and deeper degrees of relational quality, for explorative and exploitative learning.

detail.title: A Machine Learning Investigation of Spanish Law and its Relation to the Economy
detail.abstract: We investigate how the ideological content of Spanish regional laws relates to economic performance. Using the full text of all laws enacted by Spain's autonomous regions between 1981 and 2024, we construct law level polarity scores along four axes: permissiveness, liberalism, globalism, and populism, through a two-stage machine learning pipeline combining lexicon guided weak supervision with a fine tuned Spanish legal transformer. These scores are aggregated into annual region level indices, and laws are clustered into multiple sectors (social, economic, and political), allowing us to capture both the ideological tilt of legislation and the channels through which it impacts the economy. Descriptively, permissiveness and populism rise over time, while liberalism and globalism decline; dispersion increases markedly for liberalism, indicating growing cross-regional heterogeneity and polarisation. Using panel Granger-causality regressions, we find that more permissive and populist legislative flows precede slower GDP growth, particularly through the economic and social channels. Methodologically, the paper contributes a framework for large-scale measurement of ideological content in legal text, leveraging silver-label annotations to enable scalable analysis.

title: Socioeconomic and Demographic Determinants of Residential Solar Adoption in Rhode Island

detail.title: Socioeconomic and Demographic Determinants of Residential Solar Adoption in Rhode Island
detail.abstract: Despite rapid growth in residential solar deployment, adoption remains uneven across socioeconomic and demographic groups. This paper examines the structural determinants of residential solar adoption in Rhode Island using a tract-level cross-sectional analysis of 187 census tracts in the pre-2020 market. Leveraging data from Google’s Project Sunroof, the American Community Survey, and the U.S. Department of Energy, the study estimates how income, energy burden, racial composition, housing stock, and disadvantaged-community status jointly shape adoption outcomes within a uniform regulatory environment. Contrary to the standard “incentive hypothesis,” the results show that higher electricity burden is associated with significantly lower solar adoption, indicating that financial precarity functions as a barrier rather than a motivator. Housing structure emerges as the primary gatekeeper: adoption rates are significantly higher in tracts with greater shares of single-family detached homes. Interaction effects suggest that even where structural feasibility exists, disadvantaged communities convert housing potential into adoption less efficiently, pointing to complementary barriers such as credit access and housing quality. Once structural and financial constraints are accounted for, median income and racial composition lose independent explanatory power. These findings establish a pre-intervention baseline for Rhode Island’s solar market and underscore the need for policy designs that address upfront financing and structural access rather than relying solely on long-run financial incentives.

title: The Role of Trade Agreements in Preserving National Sovereignty
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Role of Trade Agreements in Preserving National Sovereignty
detail.abstract: International trade agreements are often portrayed as eroding national sovereignty. This paper argues instead that they reconstitute sovereignty as a rule-based, conditional, and continuously negotiated capacity. Distinguishing between formal sovereignty (legal authority and treaty consent) and effective sovereignty (practical policy capacity), the analysis examines how modern trade agreements structure state authority through binding commitments, regulatory exceptions, dispute settlement mechanisms, and emerging rules on digital trade and data governance. While such agreements constrain unilateral discretion in areas such as industrial policy, taxation, and regulation, they also enhance predictability, legal stability, and protection against economic coercion. Drawing on political economy and international law scholarship, the paper shows that sovereignty in the contemporary global economy is exercised less through insulation than through institutional participation, legal design, and renegotiation within a rules-based international order.

title: From the Great Depression to the Great Recession: Milton Friedman's Monetary Theory in Historical Perspective
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: From the Great Depression to the Great Recession: Milton Friedman's Monetary Theory in Historical Perspective
detail.abstract: This essay examines Milton Friedman's monetary theory in historical perspective by comparing the Great Depression and the Great Recession. Revisiting Friedman and Schwartz's monetary interpretation of the Great Depression, it emphasizes their central claim that the Federal Reserve's failure to prevent monetary contraction and banking collapse transformed a severe downturn into a prolonged catastrophe. The analysis then evaluates how this lesson shaped crisis management during the Great Recession, when central banks acted aggressively to preserve liquidity and stabilize the financial system. While these responses appear to validate Friedman's core warning against monetary passivity, the reliance on unconventional tools highlights important limitations of a framework developed for a simpler financial era. The essay argues that Friedman's enduring contribution lies not in a comprehensive theory of modern crises, but in establishing the hierarchy of crisis management: preventing monetary and banking collapse as the indispensable first task of central banking.

title: From Learning to Earning: Financial Literacy and Wealth Accumulation in the UK
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Economics

detail.title: From Learning to Earning: Financial Literacy and Wealth Accumulation in the UK
detail.abstract: Only 22% of UK households hold stocks. Even among those with substantial savings, many keep the majority of their wealth in low-yield cash accounts. This paper argues that financial-literacy frictions, not only monetary participation costs, are central to understanding who participates in equity markets and how they allocate wealth. Using the FCA Financial Lives Survey, we show that, conditional on wealth, stock-market participation is strongly increasing in financial literacy, while the share of the portfolio held in cash falls with literacy. We also document that large, early-life literacy differences across gender and education narrow with the amount invested in non-cash assets, consistent with learning-by-doing. We develop a calibrated life-cycle model in which literacy is a non-monetary participation friction that accumulates endogenously through stock-market experience. The model reproduces the imperfect wealth-participation correlation observed in the data, with some high-literacy, low-wealth households entering and some high-wealth, low literacy households remaining out. Counterfactual policy exercises show that early-life literacy interventions and stock (rather than cash) transfers can raise long-term participation, literacy, and retirement consumption, enhancing resilience to income shocks while increasing exposure to financial shocks.

title: Italian Foreign Policy In The Era Of Energy Transition: The Middle East Vector And Its Political Significance

detail.title: Italian Foreign Policy In The Era Of Energy Transition: The Middle East Vector And Its Political Significance
detail.abstract: Italy's foreign policy in the Middle East and North Africa has been closely shaped by energy security concerns, reflecting the country's limited domestic resources and its aim to enhance international influence. Historically, Italian diplomacy combined transatlantic partnership with the United States, European integration, and engagement with Mediterranean countries, allowing Rome to maintain strategic flexibility. Energy has evolved from a sectoral concern into a central element of foreign policy, linking external priorities with domestic socioeconomic needs. The national energy company ENI played a pivotal role in establishing cooperative models with oil and gas exporters, promoting equitable profit-sharing and durable political ties. Structural dependence on energy imports has guided Italy's regional focus, with cross-border electricity imports further reinforcing the importance of stable relations with neighbouring states. In the early twentyfirst century, energy considerations influenced Italy's participation in regional security initiatives and its alignment with allies. Subsequent governments emphasized diversification, engaging with Qatar, Azerbaijan, and other MENA countries, while renewable energy gained a growing share of domestic production. The Ukrainian crisis and reduction of Russian supplies accelerated diversification, positioning Algeria as the main supplier and expanding LNG imports from Qatar and the United States. Italy's Middle East and North African strategy has thus become systemic, combining import dependence, diversified sources, and infrastructure development, while using energy ties as tools of political influence and regional presence.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Incentive Theory, an axiomatic framework that treats incentives as the fundamental structuring force underlying agent behavior across economic, biological, institutional, and algorithmic systems. While existing disciplines model incentives as domain-specific variables—such as utility, fitness, payoff, or compliance—this framework elevates incentives to a primary explanatory principle. The paper formalizes the minimal conditions under which incentives exist, defines the concept of a Valid Incentive Domain, and presents a set of general laws describing how incentives shape behavior, probability of action, system stability, and long-term evolution. The framework is non-ideological and does not assume rationality, optimality, or moral alignment. Instead, it explains behavioral persistence, adaptation, and failure as emergent properties of incentive structures and their evolution over time. This working paper presents the foundational axioms and laws of the framework and outlines directions for formalization, extension, and empirical application.

detail.abstract: This paper extends the Organizational Battery Theory into the domain of the Second Law of Thermodynamics to elucidate the mechanisms governing organizational lifespan and collapse. While conventional economic models premise a frictionless law of conservation of energy (First Law), actual organizational management inevitably entails irreversible heat loss. This study defines internal organizational inefficiencies as "Entropy" and external novelty, such as technological innovation, as "Negentropy." Applying Erwin Schrödinger's definition of life, we derive the condition required for an organization's perpetuity. We conclude that organizational survival depends not merely on the residual level of financial capital (the battery) but critically on the rate of innovation (negentropy intake) sufficient to offset the relentless increase in internal entropy.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a set of general laws describing the dynamics of incentive-driven behavior within a valid incentive domain. Building on the axioms of Incentive Theory, the laws characterize how agents respond to incentive differentials, how incentive strength influences probabilistic action selection, and how multiple incentives interact over time. The laws do not assume rational choice, optimality, or deterministic decision-making. Instead, they describe incentive influence as directional and probabilistic, accommodating noise, bias, misperception, latent incentives, and structural constraints. Later laws address higher-order properties such as alignment, transparency, drift, and supersession, which govern system stability, institutional behavior, and long-run evolution. Together, the laws provide a domain-agnostic account of behavioral dynamics applicable across economic, biological, institutional, and algorithmic systems.

title:
What Can Be Predicted in Relative-Value Strategies?
A Diagnostic Framework for Convergence, Disequilibrium, and Horizon

detail.title:
What Can Be Predicted in Relative-Value Strategies?
A Diagnostic Framework for Convergence, Disequilibrium, and Horizon
detail.abstract:
Convergence-based strategies assume that mispricings revert to equilibrium—
but over what horizon, and how can this be diagnosed before capital is deployed?
This paper introduces the Stochastic Arbitrage Criterion (SAC),
which formalizes the strongest predictability admissible in relative-value
strategies without violating no-arbitrage restrictions. The key insight: while
returns are unpredictable, the persistence and horizon of latent disequilibrium
are not. A single parameter ϕ encodes market frictions, determines
convergence speed, and governs capital requirements.
The paper delivers a complete implementation framework—state-space
estimation, robustness procedures, position sizing rules—and a three-stage
decision workflow that screens strategies for arbitrage validity, horizon feasibility,
and drawdown survivability. For practitioners, this provides a diagnostic
layer that separates structural alpha from noise before capital is at
risk.

detail.abstract:
In semi-closed economic systems—characterized by varying degrees of capital restriction, regulatory compression, or geopolitical insulation—a persistent macroeconomic anomaly emerges: the economy simultaneously accumulates liquidity while losing momentum. This condition is often attributed to high interest rates or temporary uncertainty, yet it reflects a deeper structural imbalance. Excess liquidity is not inert; it exerts pressure. When effective channels for converting liquidity into initiative are absent, stagnation can persist long after conventional recessionary forces have faded.

A key but underexamined contributor to this persistence lies in the cyclical behavior of private capital. At the bottom of the economic cycle, liquidity is abundant while risk appetite remains minimal, causing idle capital to concentrate in low-risk instruments such as deposits. As growth resumes, entrepreneurial activity does increase; however, investors increasingly favor short-cycle, fast-turnover opportunities. This shift reduces private participation in long-horizon projects precisely when the economy begins to accelerate, compelling the state to assume a disproportionate share of long-cycle investment and thereby reinforcing structural inertia.

This paper develops a unified framework to explain this pattern through the interaction of three forms of capital—geographical, financial, and entrepreneurial. It demonstrates that economic motion depends less on the expansion of resources than on the reduction of structural friction among these fields. Within this architecture, the paper introduces the Synthetic Peak Mechanism: a method for reproducing key behavioral and organizational characteristics of a peak-cycle economy while the system remains near the bottom of the trough. By shifting expectations and lowering activation thresholds, the mechanism enables private capital to enter long-horizon projects earlier than would normally occur.

The central implication of the free-lunch paradox is that value can emerge not from creating additional resources, but from reordering when and how existing resources begin to move.

detail.abstract: Following the 2018 Murphy v. NCAA decision that precipitated rapid U.S. online gambling expansion, "crash" games have emerged as a popular cryptocurrency format claiming cryptographically verifiable outcomes-known in the industry as "provably fair." We analyze 20,038 rounds from an anonymized platform, testing whether game-generated multipliers conform to the theoretical distribution. Kolmogorov-Smirnov and chi-square tests detect statistically significant deviations (p < 10-15), though these are economically negligible. Following Wang and Pleimling's (2019) methodology, we estimate the probability density function exponent at α ≈ 1.98, matching the theoretical value of 2.0 and confirming fair random number generation-contrasting with their findings of α = 1.4-1.9 for player cashouts, which reflect behavioral biases rather than manipulation. Monte Carlo simulations confirm that no betting strategy produces positive returns. Session-level analysis reveals rapid loss velocity: at 179 rounds per hour, players face expected losses exceeding 500% of wagered amounts hourly. These findings support cryptographic verifiability claims while highlighting that mathematical fairness does not ensure consumer safety.

While South Korea has grappled with the lowest total fertility rate among OECD nations, the rate rebounded to 0.75 in 2024, marking the first increase in nine years. In the middle of this shift, understanding the relationship between policy initiatives and public discourse has become increasingly critical. Therefore, this study investigates the semantic positioning of fertility-related keywords in South Korean online communities across the before, during, and after COVID-19 pandemic periods. Specifically, it examines the location of these keywords on a semantic axis ranging from micro-framing to macro-framing and how the pandemic influenced these positions. Using domain fine-tuned KLUE-BERT embeddings and the semantic axis technique, we identified the semantic coordinates of key terms. Subsequently, keywords were classified into micro or macro orientations and mapped onto a quadrant analysis framework defined by two axes: pandemic shock and recovery. By applying

In a change of format, the 2014 Canadian Tax Journal introduced a new "Finances of the Nation" feature, which presents annual surveys of provincial and territorial budgets and topical articles on taxation and public expenditures in Canada. One understudied aspect of intergovernmental fiscal arrangements is the system of payments in lieu of taxes (PILT) made to local tax authorities. In light of ongoing changes to the government of Canada's real property holdings, this article reviews published federal data on PILT transfers made in 2019 to 2023 for nine cities of interest, including both cities in the National Capital Region. The article also uses city-level published data, gathered from municipal budget and fiscal documents, to assess the importance of federal PILT transfers to these municipalities. The analysis shows that the fiscal impact of PILT payments varies substantially across cities, but concludes that the PILT program is a blunt instrument that is not well suited to addressing fiscal pressures at the municipal level. The underlying data for the Finances of the Nation monographs and for the articles in this journal will be published online in the near future.

detail.abstract: This study examines the relevance of gender equity theories in explaining women's intentions to remain childless, focusing on how unequal gender arrangements in both public and private spheres shape reproductive decision-making. Using a cross-national vignette experiment conducted in 2024 (N = 9,417 women) across China, Japan, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, and the United States, respondents evaluated hypothetical scenarios varying in labor-market equality, domestic labor division, workplace support, and social norms. Results reveal striking regional contrasts: in East Asia, where childbearing remains tightly bound to marriage, unequal domestic share sharply increase intentions to remain childless, reflecting the importance of an incomplete "second gender revolution" thesis. In Western societies, however, institutional and workplace supports-not household inequality-play the central role in shaping fertility decisions. These findings demonstrate that the pathways to voluntary childlessness diverge across cultural contexts, revealing distinct mechanisms of gender inequality behind the global rise of child-free choices.

title: Beyond Price: A Technical Quality Framework for AI Antitrust

detail.title: Beyond Price: A Technical Quality Framework for AI Antitrust
detail.abstract: Disruptive and nascent competitors in the artificial intelligence (AI) market are uniquely positioned to exploit the wide margin for innovation and explore multiple innovation trajectories. However, incumbent tech firms are increasingly dominating the AI landscape to protect their platforms. These firms can aggressively compete for market share while offering AI models and tools at subsidized prices to maintain users on their platforms, making antitrust frameworks focused on price effects inadequate for detecting anticompetitive behavior. To address this gap, we propose a technically informed framework for antitrust analysis that leverages established benchmarks and quality metrics: the Technical Qualities and Metrics Vector (TQMV). This framework offers a pathway to operationalize quality rather than price effects, allowing for more nuanced definitions of relevant markets and better quantification of the competitive effects of transactions such as "acquihires." We illustrate through case studies how this framework can inform antitrust analysis. More broadly, our paper lays the foundation for interdisciplinary work at the intersection of computer science, AI, and law that examines competitive dynamics and the role of antitrust enforcement in this new market.

title: Dedollarization and the Wane of Western Sanctions

detail.title: Dedollarization and the Wane of Western Sanctions
detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes the growing momentum behind dedollarization efforts and their implications for the long term effectiveness of Western sanctions. Focusing on recent developments in global energy markets and financial settlement practices the paper examines how countries including Russia China India and key Middle Eastern states are increasingly adopting alternative currencies and payment mechanisms to reduce exposure to United States sanctions. Using open source policy analysis the paper traces the expansion of non dollar energy trade including settlements conducted in yuan dirhams and local currencies as well as the development of parallel financial messaging systems outside of the SWIFT framework.

The analysis argues that the unprecedented scale and speed of sanctions imposed on Russia following the invasion of Ukraine has accelerated incentives for governments in Asia and the Middle East to pursue dedollarization as a form of strategic risk mitigation. These efforts are reinforced by concerns over future sanctions exposure monetary tightening in the United States and the desire of major emerging economies to internationalize their currencies. The paper concludes that while dedollarization does not signal the imminent collapse of the dollar centered financial system it does represent a structural shift that is likely to weaken the coercive power of sanctions over time particularly in energy markets and South South trade. The findings contribute to broader debates on financial statecraft sanctions efficacy and the evolving architecture of the international monetary system.

title: (Mis)Measuring Uncertainty: Bunching in Probabilistic Expectations
affiliations: Universidad de Barcelona, Banco de España - Research Department, Banco de España and Banco de España

detail.title: (Mis)Measuring Uncertainty: Bunching in Probabilistic Expectations
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the measurement of uncertainty through probabilistic expectation survey questions (PESQ). We focus on bunching, defined as the allocation of 100% probability to a single scenario. Taken at face-value, bunching implies perfect certainty, but we consider the possibility that it instead represents a form of measurement error driven by the cognitive burden of the task. We bring five pieces of evidence to support this hypothesis using data from two distinct surveys that contain similar probabilistic questions: the ECB Consumer Expectations Survey (ECB-CES) and the Spanish Survey of Household Finances (EFF in its Spanish acronym). Using CES, we first document a negative gradient between financial literacy and bunching. Second, we show that bunching increases with panel tenure, consistent with survey fatigue. Third, exploiting a within-fieldwork intervention in the EFF, we show that enforcing strict interviewer protocols causally reduces bunching by 15 percentage points. Fourth, we provide causal evidence that structural changes to the questionnaire design further reduce bunching by 18 percentage points relative to the CES baseline. Finally, we document that standardization minimizes interviewer variance. Together, these findings highlight the importance of response effects, rather than certainty, in driving bunching, suggesting that standard PESQ measures likely overstate subjective certainty.

detail.title: The Implementation of the Philippine National Police (PNP) Anti-Illegal Drugs Campaign Plan-Project: Double Barrel in the Province of Misamis Oriental
detail.abstract:
This study assessed the implementation of the PNP anti-illegal drugs campaign plan project on double barrel in the province of Misamis Oriental considering Project Tokhang and Project High Value (HVT). It also sought the problems encountered by PNP in the implementation of the above-named programs.
This descriptive study involved 150 participants from the PNP members of the Provincial Police Office of the Province of Misamis Oriental. It made a researcher-made instrument and the interview technique in gathering the data.
Findings show that (1) Project Tokhang and the different stages of its implementation got a rating of well implemented. Similarly, Project HVT and the different procedures of its implementation are also well implemented. (2) The problems encountered included the following: inadequate financial and logistic support for its operation; lack of active participation of drug surrenderers in activities which resulted in the delay of compliance with the requirements for the declaration of barangay as drug-free; the lack of participation of Barangay Anti-Drug Abuse Council (BADAC) due to political reasons which resulted in the delay of the submission of drug watch list, and lack of initiative for the conduct of Community-Based Rehabilitation Program (CBRP) activities which led to the delay in compliance with requirements for the declaration of barangay as drug-free; and the lack of active participation of the community to serve as witnesses against drug personalities for legal apprehension and hesitance to give information about the background of drug personalities.
The study concluded that most of PNP have complied with all the stages in the implementation of the project tokhang and they followed the protocols, guidelines, procedures and Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) indicated in the Revised Manual on Anti-Illegal Drugs and Investigation. Problems on the implementation of double barrel did not affect the performance of the PNP personnel. Therefore, it can be concluded that they found ways and means to sustain the program in compliance of the mandates to avoid administrative sanctions.

title: Freedoms, Agency and Colombian State Organization

detail.title: Freedoms, Agency and Colombian State Organization

The central objective is to evaluate whether the Colombian state structure, in its constitutional design, effectively contributes to freedoms both as an end-the substantive expansion of capabilities-and as a means-instruments that enable other social, economic, and political achievements.

detail.abstract: This article analyzes the separate-entity approach as the theoretical basis of the arm’s-length principle in the transfer-pricing guidelines of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Despite its central role, the concept lacks a clear definition, and its application appears to fluctuate between transactional, entity-level, and group-wide perspectives, potentially calling into question an unequivocal reliance on the approach as the theoretical basis of the arm’s-length principle in the OECD guidelines. The purpose of this article is to analyze the definition and application of the separate-entity approach in the OECD guidelines, with the aim of clarifying its meaning, identifying potential deviations from a strictly entity-based analysis, and examining the rationale, if any, behind such deviations. The first conclusion of the study is that article 9 of the OECD model tax convention, which underpins the arm’s-length principle, does not impose a legal requirement to analyze transactions strictly at the level of individual legal entities. Rather, it supports a flexible interpretation aimed at ensuring that related-party transactions reflect market-based profits. The second conclusion is that the OECD guidelines need to address complex group structures and intragroup arrangements that may not exist between unrelated parties, while remaining within the realm of the arm’s-length principle. This paradox leads to the adoption of various perspectives—transactional, entity-based, and group-wide—to better approximate the conditions that may exist between independent enterprises. The need for such flexibility reflects the difficulty of applying a market-based standard in a non-market setting.

detail.abstract: Nations compete among themselves in various forms. Increasingly, tax policy is one such area, as countries seek to attract to themselves economic activity (and resulting benefits such as jobs and tax revenue) that exists (or could be created in) other countries, while retaining such economic activity as already exists within its borders. Never has economic activity been so skewed toward services and digital forms that have less and less physical connection to any particular jurisdiction and are increasingly capable of moving from one country to another. America’s 2025 tariff outburst reflects the accelerating weaponization of tax systems within the larger competition among nations, and the United States in particular has shown itself quite willing to use various tax incentives and disincentives to shape both private sector decision making (within and outside its borders) and the policy choices of other countries. This article examines the past and present state of international tax competition among various different forms of taxation.

detail.abstract: Canada’s retirement income system requires modernization. In 2025, old age security (OAS) will deliver over $18,000 annually to retired couples with household incomes of $182,000, while still leaving almost 400,000 older Canadians below the poverty line. At a cost of $86 billion per year, OAS is the largest federal transfer and the biggest source of new spending growth, driving the operating deficit. Younger Canadians now contribute 20-40 percent more in income taxes toward seniors’ healthy retirements than baby boomers once paid, while programs for housing, child care, and postsecondary education receive relatively little new money. Drawing on the reform blueprint advanced by Prime Minister Chrétien in the mid1990s, a recent auditor general review, and new microsimulation modelling, this article evaluates six policy options to recalibrate OAS recovery thresholds and phase out the age and pension income tax credits. The analysis shows that redirecting benefits from financially secure retirees with six-figure incomes could free up $14 billion to $19 billion annually—enough to eliminate seniors’ poverty, expand investments in younger generations, and reduce the deficit without raising taxes. These reforms to retirement income security would be a textbook case of “better late than never” to advance multiple priorities in Prime Minister Carney’s mandate letter.

detail.abstract: For almost 60 years, the Canadian Tax Foundation published an annual monograph, Finances of the Nation, and its predecessor, The National Finances. In a change of format, the 2014 Canadian Tax Journal introduced a new "Finances of the Nation" feature, which presents annual surveys of provincial and territorial budgets and topical articles on taxation and public expenditures in Canada. This article examines implications of the global financial cycle for Canada's public sector borrowers, with a particular emphasis on the borrowing conditions of Canadian provinces. It makes three broad points. First, even relative to other advanced economies, Canada, and the government of Canada in particular, has done well by the global financial cycle. In a world of trade imbalances and uncertainty, investors need safe assets, and Canada's wealth, political stability, and open capital markets have made government of Canada bonds a natural haven. Second, the provinces have also done well by the global financial cycle, but their bonds are riskier and less liquid than government of Canada debt, which explains why their spreads tend to increase with global volatility, and why, if volatility becomes too severe, the provinces occasionally struggle to borrow. Volatility-related premiums are lower among provinces with relatively large and liquid pools of debt, and higher-if the volatility is associated with a significant drop in oil prices-among oil-producing provinces. Third, the global financial cycle is evolving, and one of the most important developments is the growing vulnerability of central governments. Sovereign bond yields no longer reliably fall in the face of adverse conditions, and in some cases they even increase. These developments appear to stem from a combination of technical factors and growing concerns about sovereign credit risk, particularly in the United States. They also represent a fundamental shift in the pricing of traditionally safe assets and expose the government of Canada and provinces to a number of unknown risks. The underlying data for the Finances of the Nation monographs and for the articles in this journal will be published online in the near future.

detail.abstract: The release in 2016 by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development of a draft multilateral treaty to modify thousands of global bilateral tax treaties was met with surprisingly strong support by the international community, with many states signing, ratifying, and implementing the treaty. One of the treaty’s most contentious elements is the addition to the dispute resolution measures in bilateral treaties, a process known as mutual agreement procedure, of a mandatory arbitration procedure that is to be available where agreement cannot be reached under the conventional process. In contrast to the mutual agreement procedure, which includes no requirement that a final agreement be reached, the mandatory arbitration procedure can provide a guaranteed resolution of a treaty dispute. Although the arbitration article has been ratified by most developed countries, many developing nations have noted reservations to it, indicating that they will not incorporate it into their bilateral treaties. Central to the many arguments that have been put forward by opponents of mandatory arbitration in bilateral tax treaties is the argument that agreeing to mandatory arbitration would amount to an unacceptable surrender of sovereignty. However, when viewed critically in the context of tax treaties, this and many other concerns fall away or are revealed to be red herring arguments. A better view, this article suggests, is that entering into a tax treaty is an exercise of fiscal sovereignty, and any agreement to reduce taxing or other rights in the treaty should be seen as an element of that exercise of sovereignty to gain the benefits or advantages the parties seek through a treaty that grants mutual rights to and imposes mutual obligations on sovereign signatories.

detail.abstract: Students often struggle with the marginal concept in economics due to the intuitive disconnection between calculus and human behavior. This lecture note bridges the gap by mapping economic concepts onto kinematics: utility is position, consumption is time, marginal utility is speed, and price is stream speed. The Lagrange multiplier receives a fresh interpretation as the Mach number of consumption. The analogy is developed through two examples: the Amtrak Empire Service train diagram illustrates speed as slope, and the Maid of the Mist boat excursion illustrates utility maximization as navigating against a river stream. At optimum, every dollar achieves the same Mach across all markets; high Mach indicates tight budget, low Mach indicates relaxed budget.

detail.title: Inflation and Competition in an Old Keynesian Model
detail.abstract: I study how rationing affects endogenous competition and real rigidities. Households search for firms in the goods market. Nominal rigidities prevent firms from clearing excess demand, incentivizing firms to ration by rejecting buyers. Under excess supply, the model resembles standard New Keynesian models as few firms ration. Under excess demand, however, my model differs substantially. First, rationing, particularly by low-price firms, impedes price competition and matching efficiency. Both elasticity and superelasticity fall, fueling inflation by raising markups and relaxing real rigidities. Second, endogenous competition creates strong nonlinearity in the Phillips curve  and asymmetric inflation persistence without menu costs or changes in concentration. Inflation is higher and more persistent after inflationary shocks, and these effects are not confined to large shocks. Third, stable markups cause real wages to stagnate even in an overheated economy. This partially explains the absence of wage-price spirals during COVID despite tight labor markets. Finally, I provide empirical evidence on rationing and endogenous real rigidities.

detail.abstract: The Canadian job market faces a significant transition as a result of the advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technology and a new approach to tariffs and trade by the US administration. Without meaningful change in domestic policy, an increase in unemployment rates may have a negative impact on Canada’s economy, communities, and the health and well-being of individuals. In this article, we review prior studies to develop a framework that allows us to map the probable impacts of unemployment levels on economies, communities, and individual wellness outcomes. We analyze the potential impact of tariffs and AI adoption on the Canadian job market between 2025 and 2030 using scenario analysis, and find that the most likely outcome is an unemployment rate peaking above 9 percent. Addressing this challenge requires an integrated approach across government policies, including tax policy, to strengthen the economic pillars supporting business enterprises, to advance the development of skills and training, and to drive the creation of enterprise value by employing Canadian talent. We identify critical success factors for corporate tax incentives, suggest prospective policies, and recommend bold policy changes to elevate investment in human capital and help Canada to thrive in an era of AI and tariffs.

detail.abstract: Measured financial knowledge declined by 15 percent in the U.S. between 2009 and 2021. We propose one possible explanation: an increase in smartphone responses on web-based surveys. Using within-individual variation in device type in a representative internet panel, we first observe that when respondents use smartphones, they are more likely to choose “don’t know” and less likely to answer questions correctly than when responding on a desktop, laptop, or tablet. We then conduct an experiment where respondents are randomized to complete a survey on a smartphone or another device and find remarkably similar results. Leveraging randomized question placement, we find that the smartphone penalty is larger when questions appear later in the survey. We find similar results for a set of general knowledge questions. Back-ofthe- envelope calculations suggest that at least 23 percent of the decline in financial knowledge can be attributable to expanded smartphone use when taking surveys.

detail.abstract: Competitive markets are often expected to reward firms that focus on long-term value creation. In reality, many firms operating under intense competition persistently adopt strategies that weaken long-term unit economics, even when decision-makers are aware of these costs. This paper examines why such behavior continues and argues that short-term value destruction can arise as a rational outcome of competitive incentives rather than managerial failure. The analysis focuses on how relative performance evaluation and incentive pressure shape firm behavior. In markets where firms are constantly compared using short-term, observable metrics such as growth, order volume, or market share, deviation from these benchmarks can trigger immediate penalties. These penalties are often more visible and severe than the uncertain benefits of long-term discipline. As a result, firms may rationally prioritize maintaining competitive position in the short run even when doing so delays profitability or erodes margins. To ground this argument, the paper examines competition in the Indian food delivery sector, with particular attention to the rivalry between Swiggy and Zomato. This market is characterized by low switching costs, high price sensitivity, and strong scale effects, conditions under which short-term customer acquisition becomes a dominant competitive signal. Both firms have repeatedly relied on aggressive discounting and promotional pricing to defend market share and order volume. While these strategies succeed in attracting users in the short run, they compress margins and delay sustainable profitability, a tradeoff that has been widely acknowledged in public disclosures and investor commentary. Despite this awareness, discount-driven competition persists. This paper argues that such behavior reflects a coordination problem created by competitive incentives. Unilateral restraint is costly, as firms that reduce discounts risk rapid customer loss and negative signaling to investors, partners, and the market. Even when margins improve temporarily, reduced scale can weaken bargaining power and long-term efficiency. Competitive pressure therefore locks firms into an equilibrium where short-term signaling dominates, even when it produces inferior long-term outcomes. By examining firm behavior through the lens of incentives and relative evaluation, this paper highlights why market outcomes can diverge from long-term value maximization. Apparent short-termism in business strategy often reflects rational responses to competitive constraints rather than flawed decision-making.

detail.abstract: Improving energy efficiency in the residential sector and shifting away from fossil fuel-based heating are crucial for achieving net-zero energy systems. Here, we present empirically grounded projections of the demand for low-carbon energy technologies among private households. Using a nationwide discrete-choice experiment involving 1,676 homeowners from all regions of Switzerland, we examine how technology demand is influenced by subsidies and peer effects. We find substantial demand among homeowners for capital-intensive, decentralized technologies, such as rooftop photovoltaic systems, envelope retrofits, and heat pumps, which can be increased further through subsidies. In contrast, subsidies have little impact on the demand for centralized technologies. Electricity storage solutions are generally not attractive to homeowners unless they are combined with other technologies. At the current speed of technology adoption, peer effects will play a minor role in stimulating technology demand, even when technologies are heavily subsidized. This calls for further efforts to remove the barriers to technology adoption that currently hinder the spread of technologies through peer influence.

detail.abstract: Banks play a crucial role in the transition towards a more sustainable global economy by directing capital flows to sustainable activities. Drawing on the management control system (MCS) framework of Malmi and Brown (2008), this study analyses 17 semi-structured interviews with individuals at from five Swiss banks to examine how sustainability is integrated into banks’ MCSs and how this integration is shaped by internal and external drivers. We show that the integration of sustainability into business strategy, administrative controls, and organizational culture, as well as into top-management commitment constitute important levers to change banks’ core business activities, both directly and through their MCSs. Furthermore, we observe substantial variation in how sustainability is integrated across these levers and across different MCS components, which translates into varying degrees of sustainability integration in lending and investment products. Regarding external drivers, regulation induces banks to formally integrate sustainability into client advisory processes and reporting, yet does not necessarily induce fundamental organizational change. Sustainability reporting plays a dual role: while externally mandated, reporting requirements support internal integration by defining the relevant data points. Overall, our findings highlight the dynamic and interconnected nature of sustainability integration in banks and underscore that banks can actively shape their transformation.

detail.abstract: Australia saw major tax reform at the end of the millennium, and the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax acted as the catalyst that created opportunities for me to move from industry to academia. detail.abstract: Necessity is the mother of invention, they say. Since ancient times, humanity has continued to strive for its unique quest for knowledge. With each progress, they introduced new dimensions for amusements and recreational purposes, which the millennials quote as an adrenaline rush. One such path-breaking invention is the concept of space tourism as an adventure for the rich. Space tourism, in simplest terms, refers to travelling into space for adventure. History was made by one Dannis A. Tito, who travelled to space in 2001, known as the first man to make his first space voyage as a space tourist. Once the ambit of space tourism emerged, the need for a legal framework to regulate such transits was also felt. Thereby, Space law developed as a new discipline to govern the growing aspects of space tourism. This paper aims to discuss the concept of Space tourism and the concurrent space laws that regulate such activities. This paper also focuses on the impact of space tourism in modern civilised nations and the responsibilities of the States in regulating space tourism. While discussing the relationship between tourists, operators, and third parties, this paper also discusses their liabilities toward each other in case of probable dangers. This paper also discusses the current status of Space tourism and space law within the legal framework of various International Treaties.

title: The Coronavirus Trade-off --Life vs. Economy: Handling the Trade-off Rationally and Optimally

detail.title: The Coronavirus Trade-off --Life vs. Economy: Handling the Trade-off Rationally and Optimally
detail.abstract: The recent coronavirus outbreak has made governments face an inconvenient trade-off choice, i.e. the choice between saving lives and saving the economy, forcing them to make immensely consequential decisions among alternative courses of actions without knowing what the ultimate results would be for the society as a whole. This paper attempts to frame the coronavirus trade-off problem as an economic optimization problem and proposes mathematical optimization methods to make rationally optimal decisions when faced with trade-off situations such as those involved in managing through the recent coronavirus pandemic. The framework introduced and the method proposed in this paper are on the basis of the theory of rational choice at a societal level, which assumes that the government is a rational, benevolent agent that systematically and purposefully takes into account the social marginal costs and social marginal benefits of its actions to its citizens and makes decisions that maximize the society's well-being as a whole. We approach solving this trade-off problem from a static as well as a dynamic point of view. Finally, we provide several numerical examples clarifying how the proposed framework and methods can be applied in the real-world context.

detail.abstract: The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) came into force on 1 October 2023, introducing reporting requirements for importers of covered products and, from 2026, an obligation to pay a fee on the carbon content of imported goods. This paper uses indices of ad valorem tariffs to assess the incidence of the EU CBAM on both EU member states and the EU’s trading partners. Overall, the direct impact on EU countries’ trade is estimated to be small, adding 0.1 percent to the value of EU imports when averaged across all imports, and 0.04 percent to the average cost of non-EU countries’ exports to the EU—with a maximum of 1.2 percent. detail.title: The ‘Ascension’ Strategy for Canadian Labour Law Reform: Options for Broader based Collective Bargaining
detail.abstract: In Canada, as in many other countries, collective bargaining coverage has fallen sharply since the 1980s. While there is widespread understanding that a labour law model designed in the 1930s is probably no longer fit for purposes in the 21st century, there is little agreement on what a revised, modern collective bargaining law should look like. The possibilities for "broader-based" bargaining models are often bandied about in policy circles, but there is little understanding or agreement on what those models would do or how they would operate in practice. In this Working Paper, I describe a model for thinking about modern labour law reform that involves strategies of "ascension" and "descension" from the Wagner model's focus on enterprise bargaining.  The paper then describes various models of broader-based bargaining that have been proposed or adopted in western nations that have traditionally relied on decentralized models of collective bargaining. The paper concludes with a call for governments to study broader-based bargaining in a serious attempt to map a way forward for collective bargaining in the 21st century.

detail.title: Milton Friedman's Spending Matrix Revisited: 'Spending Efficiency' and 'Preference Compatibility' Across different Economic Systems
detail.abstract: This article expands Milton Friedman's spending matrix to analyse 'spending efficiency' and 'preference compatibility' across different economic systems against five key outcome criteria. By generalising Friedman's typology, it compares efficiency and freedom as systems shift from laissez-faire capitalism to communism, illustrating a gradual deterioration in their key outcomes. While government intervention is sometimes necessary to address market failures, its role should always be carefully limited to avoid inefficiency and misalignment with individual preferences. The insights may provide guidance for policymakers in designing economic systems and policies that promote both economic prosperity and personal liberty.

detail.abstract: The article focuses on the theoretical and legal analysis of jus cogens norms as a universal constraint on immunities in the context of the case law of the European Court of Human Rights and the International Criminal Court. The aim of the study is to reveal the legal nature of jus cogens norms as a universal limitation on immunities and a guarantee of effective justice in cases involving violations of the fundamental principles of international law. The study employed general scientific methods of cognition: analysis, synthesis, induction, deduction, abstraction, generalization and the comparative legal method. The findings show that jus cogens norms are being established as a fundamental category of international public law with absolute legal authority and priority over both customary rules and international treaties. Their imperative nature imposes restrictions not only on lawmaking but also on the application of the concepts of state and functional immunity in cases involving crimes against the core values of humanity. The case law of the International Criminal Court, specialized tribunals, and, to some extent, the European Court of Human Rights has been analyzed, demonstrating a gradual limitation of the scope of immunities in cases involving crimes falling under jus cogens. It is emphasized that this trend reinforces the primacy of victims’ rights and strengthens the principle of unconditional accountability. The conclusion highlights the need to reform Ukraine’s criminal procedural legislation in order to implement jus cogens norms. It is shown that such reform should include the introduction of special proceedings for individuals with immunity, the priority of peremptory norms over national limitations, and the creation of effective procedural mechanisms for investigating and prosecuting crimes that threaten international legal order. It has been proven that the law must provide for the possibility of prosecuting individuals regardless of their official status or citizenship, and the judiciary must apply jus cogens norms as universal standards that cannot be overridden by references to national privileges. This approach aligns with Ukraine’s international obligations and promotes the strengthening of the rule of law at all levels. The practical value of the study lies in developing a normative framework to ensure effective accountability for jus cogens crimes within the Ukrainian jurisdiction.

title: Global Financial Spillovers of U.S. Trade Policy

detail.title: Global Financial Spillovers of U.S. Trade Policy
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the dynamic transmission of U.S. trade policy shocks to the macro-financial conditions of 26 major trading partners using a country-specific structural vector autoregression framework spanning January 2001 to June 2025. We document a distinct heterogeneity in global spillovers characterized by a tug-of-war between opposing economic forces. For economies deeply integrated into North American supply chains, such as Australia, Chile, and Colombia, U.S. tariffs manifest as stagflationary cost-push shocks. Conversely, for major Eurozone exporters like Germany, Austria, and Italy, the deflationary demand channel prevails, as negative income effects outweigh cost pressures. Beyond price dynamics, we uncover a rapid financial transmission channel where trade policy functions as a primary driver of asset repricing. While the shocks trigger immediate equity sell-offs in markets such as Sweden and France, we observe large positive cumulative returns in Canada, consistent with trade diversion effects. Cross-country regressions identify the structural determinants of this variation: financial openness and global value chain participation significantly mitigate short-run exchange rate depreciation, whereas geographic distance and import dependence amplify long-run asset price volatility. Quantitatively, trade policy uncertainty explains over 27\% of the forecast error variance in Canadian stock returns, highlighting the dominance of U.S. policy in driving partner financial conditions. These findings underscore a monetary policy dilemma, where central banks in emerging markets must tighten rates to defend currencies against capital flight despite sharply tightening financial conditions.

The objective of this research was to study the relationship between the participation of the elderly in learning programs in cultural activities developed in senior centers. The research was quantitative, cross-sectional and relational; a probabilistic sample was applied to select 340 elderly people over 65 years of age, corresponding to a senior center in Madrid. The instrument used to collect information consisted of 20 questions grouped into 4 dimensions. The results indicate that the elderly are satisfied with the new cultural learning offered by  the senior centers. 72% of the people surveyed, contribute to improve learning through these activities. The research provides possible improvements to prevent loneliness, improving the quality of life. It is suggested to improve the learning programs in cultural activities to achieve greater participation in society. This research suggests possible improvements in areas that will help prevent dependency, such as those where there is greater demand from users. Specific plans to increase the participation of men in the workshops held in the senior centers are suggested as suggestions for improvement.
