detail.abstract:
Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major public health challenge in Azerbaijan, where stigma and discrimination continue to act as significant barriers to timely diagnosis, access to care, and treatment adherence. This national TB Stigma Assessment aimed to evaluate the extent, forms, and drivers of TB-related stigma across multiple settings and population groups, and to identify legal, social, and health-system factors contributing to stigma. Using standardized tools developed by the Stop TB Partnership, the study employed a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative surveys and qualitative data collection.

Data were collected between October and December 2023 from 540 participants across nearly all economic regions of Azerbaijan, including people with TB (PWTB), family members, community members, health care workers, and key stakeholders. Quantitative data were analyzed using SPSS, while qualitative findings were triangulated through focus group discussions and legal and policy review.

The findings reveal high levels of self-stigma among PWTB (51%), widespread stigma within communities (69%), and notable stigma within health care settings (57%). More than one-third of PWTB reported experiencing enacted stigma, particularly in communities, workplaces, and health facilities, often during the early stages of the TB care pathway. Women with TB were disproportionately affected across most stigma dimensions. Family members and health care workers also reported experiencing secondary stigma.

The assessment concludes that addressing TB stigma requires comprehensive legal reform, community awareness, health worker training, and people-centered support services to improve health outcomes.

detail.title: Evaluating Behavioral Interventions at Scale with AI
detail.abstract: We test the effectiveness of different AI-delivered conversation protocols to increase people's motivation for change. In a large-scale experiment with 2,719 social media users, we randomly assign participants to a control conversation or one of three treatment arms: two Motivational Interviewing protocols promoting self-persuasion (change focus or decisional balance) and a direct persuasion protocol providing unsolicited advice and information. All conversations are led by an AI interviewer, enabling standardized delivery of each protocol at scale. Our results show that all three interventions significantly increase motivation for change and the perceived costs of social media use, with change-focused self-persuasion yielding the largest effects. These effects persist and translate into self-reported reductions in social media use more than two weeks after the intervention. Our findings illustrate how AI-led conversations can serve as a scalable platform both for delivering behavioral interventions and for testing what makes them effective by systematically varying how conversations are conducted.

detail.abstract: The goal of this paper is to investigate the importance of providing visual "big pictures" in the teaching of economics. The plurality and variety of concepts, variables, diagrams, and models involved in economics can be a source of confusion for many economics students. However, reviewing the existing literature on the importance of providing visual "big pictures" in the process of learning suggests that furnishing students with a visual "big picture" that illustrates the ways through which those numerous, diverse concepts are connected to each other could be an effective solution to clear up the mentioned mental chaos. As a practical example, this paper introduces a "big picture" that can be used as a good resource in intermediate macroeconomics classes. This figure presents twenty-seven commonly-discussed macroeconomic diagrams in the intermediate macroeconomics course, and gives little detail on some of these diagrams, aiming at helping students to get the whole picture at once on a single piece of paper. This macroeconomics big picture mostly focuses on the routes through which common diagrams in macroeconomics are connected to each other, and finally introduces the general macroeconomic equilibrium that is graphically derived through those connections.

title: Historicism and Urban Climate Governance in the Americas

detail.title: Historicism and Urban Climate Governance in the Americas

detail.abstract: As climate risks become increasingly apparent in cities and other urban areas, there is a growing need to develop climate mitigation and adaptation strategies to reduce the vulnerability of people and communities in such geographies. While the literature on urban climate governance emphasizes contemporary policies and future projections, it often overlooks the historical context that shapes present-day urban climates and the increasingly vital role that historical knowledge plays in climate mitigation and adaptation efforts. In addition, existing studies tend to neglect the deep-rooted historical factors that have shaped urban governance structures themselves. Meanwhile, there is a lack of methodological frameworks that adequately capture the complex qualitative interplay between historical processes and contemporary climate governance practices. This study addresses these gaps in the literature by exploring the role that historicism plays in urban climate governance. Drawing upon the theories and approaches of political ecology, historicism, and global governance, and utilizing quantitative and qualitative content analysis methods, this paper examines how cities in the Americas are building resilience to climate change by fusing historical knowledge with ecological principles. Moreover, by paying greater attention to historicism in environmental analysis and solutionsfinding, this study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of how historical legacies influence urban climate governance strategies and outcomes. The empirics for this study were gathered from an analysis of climate plans and green urban development projects (N=102) enacted between 2001 and 2020 in climate hotspot cities (N=95) located in North America, Latin America, and Caribbean island states. The findings of this study confirm that city planners and urban development plans in these regions are increasingly incorporating historical knowledge as they address the issue of climate change. Much of the historical and ecological knowledge systems that are being incorporated into urban planning aim to remedy historical legacies of socioeconomic inequity, which manifest contemporarily as environmental and spatial inequalities (or vice versa) in these cities. These legacies of inequality are shown to disproportionately concentrate climate risks in neighborhoods and communities that have been historically underserved and resource-strapped. The typologies of climate risk interventions where these historical knowledge systems were being applied were evenly distributed between nature-based and governance interventions. However, green infrastructural development, water resource management, and native biodiversity enhancement were the main intervention areas these plans addressed. Plans also focused more on climate adaptation in South America and the Caribbean island states, whereas climate mitigation (carbon emissions reduction) featured more prominently in the plans of North American cities. The unavailability of historical data on certain aspects of city ecology was a major limitation identified in these climate plans. This study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of the complex interactions between the past, present, and future that are shaping cities in the face of global climate shifts.

detail.abstract: Marketing houses using the pre-project selling (PPS) system is prone to problems because the houses being marketed are not yet completed, so that losses suffered by consumers due to developer default can have an impact on property agents who act as intermediaries between developers and consumers in marketing houses using the PPS system. The purpose of this study is to analyse the legal relationship between developers, property agents, and consumers, as well as the legal responsibility of property agents in marketing houses using the PPS system. The research method used was empirical legal research in the city of Makassar. The data sources consisted of primary data (interviews) and secondary data (laws and regulations, books, and other literature). Data collection techniques were conducted through interviews and literature studies, then analysed qualitatively through descriptive descriptions. The results of the study show that the legal relationship between developers and real estate agents, and developers and consumers, is bound by agreement. Meanwhile, real estate agents and consumers do not have a direct legal relationship, because real estate agents only act as intermediaries between developers and consumers. Real estate agents are not included in the sale and purchase agreement between developers and consumers. Therefore, in general, real estate agents are not directly responsible for developers' default in the PPS system. However, property agents still have a moral responsibility to consumers in the event of default by developers. The conclusion of this study is that the legal relationship between developers, property agents, and consumers gives rise to the rights and obligations of each party according to their position. If each party understands this, then house marketing using the PPS system can run well without harming any party.

detail.title: Assessing the Relative Importance of the Drivers of CO2 Emissions in the Selected Emerging Economies Using Machine Learning Approach
detail.abstract: The main objective of the present research is to answer a key research question: what is the relative importance of the drivers of CO2 emissions? Another important question the present study addresses is how the countries are related to each other regarding CO2 emissions. Taking a sample of 42 emerging economies from Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) and using hierarchical clustering and the neural network method the study tries to answer the key question. Firstly, the explanatory variables were identified through a review of the literature. Subsequently, the gathered data was classified into two clusters having similar characteristic variables utilizing the dendrogram by performing an exploratory clustering method known as hierarchical clustering. Later using the machine learning K-Means clustering technique, the clusters were verified. The use of another machine learning method of feed-forward multilayer perceptron commonly known as neural network helped us to identify the relative importance of explanatory variables viz. economic growth (EG), renewable energy consumption (REC), urbanization (URB), democracy index (DI) and foreign direct investment (FDI) for their relation to the response variable viz. CO2 emissions. The neural network results reveal that EG, REC, and URB are the most important variables (with Rank 1,2, and 3 respectively) followed by DI (Rank 4) and FDI (Rank 5). FDI seemingly is the least important among these identified variables.

title: Econometric Modeling of Input-Driven Output Risk through a Versatile CES Production Function

detail.title: Econometric Modeling of Input-Driven Output Risk through a Versatile CES Production Function
detail.abstract: The conventional functional form of the Constant-Elasticity-of-Substitution (CES) production function is a general production function nesting a number of other forms of production functions. Examples of such functions include Leontief, Cobb-Douglas, and linear production functions. Nevertheless, the conventional form of the CES production specification is still restrictive in multiple aspects. One example is the fact that the marginal effect of increasing input use always has to be to increase the variability of output quantity by the conventional construction of this function. This paper proposes a generalized variant of the CES production function that allows for various input effects on the probability distribution of output. Failure to allow for this possible input-output risk structure is indeed one of the limitations of the conventional form of the CES production function. This limitation may result in false inferences about input-driven output risk. In light of this, the present paper proposes a solution to this problem. First, it is shown that the familiar CES formulation suffers from very restrictive structural assumptions regarding risk considerations, and that such restrictions may lead to biased and inefficient estimates of production quantity and production risk. Following the general theme of Just and Pope's approach, a CES-based production-function specification that overcomes this shortcoming of the original CES production function is introduced, and a three-stage Nonlinear Least-Squares (NLS) estimation procedure for the estimation of the proposed functional form is presented. To illustrate the proposed approaches in this paper, two empirical applications in irrigation and fertilizer response using the famous Hexem-Heady experimental dataset are provided. Finally, implications for modeling input-driven production risks are discussed.

title: The African Regional Human and Peoples' Rights System: 40 Years of Progress and Challenges

detail.title: The African Regional Human and Peoples' Rights System: 40 Years of Progress and Challenges
detail.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to provide a comprehensive and detailed analysis of the African regional human rights system, emphasizing both its innovations and remaining challenges. To this end, a literature review of primary sources, as well as the jurisprudence of the human rights bodies of the African system, will be analyzed. Although this system did not start functioning until the decade of the eighties of the 20th century, it has evolved considerably once the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights was adopted. Thus, several other treaties followed it, of which the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child and the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples› Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa can be pointed out. And even though initially only the creation of protection and control mechanisms was foreseen-the African Commission on Human and People's Rights and the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child-after 1998, the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights was added, which has progressively adopted a protectionist and growing jurisprudence; but also that, as its predecessors, will face different challenges, among which the reform process of the judicial bodies of the African Union themselves. In any case, the main conclusion of this article is that the innovations of the system are considerable (and largely unknown), although outstanding challenges need to be addressed to ensure the effectiveness and development of the system.

title: Backward Growth Accounting: An Economic Tool for Strategic Planning of Business Growth

detail.title: Backward Growth Accounting: An Economic Tool for Strategic Planning of Business Growth
detail.abstract: Business growth is a goal of great importance for its both private and social benefits. Many firms view business growth as an imperative for their survival, stability, and long-term success. Business growth can be socially beneficial, too, as it enables businesses to expand into new territories where they can stimulate economic growth and development, creates more jobs, increase living standards, and better serve their communities by giving back more through Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives. Business growth must be planned reasonably and optimally so that it can effectively achieve its critical ambitions in business practice. The current common practices for planning the supply side of business growth are usually ad-hoc and lack well-established mathematical and economic foundations. The present paper argues that business growth planning can be pursued more structurally, reliably, and meaningfully within the framework of Growth Accounting (GA), which was first introduced by Economics Nobel Laureate Robert Solow to study economic growth. It is shown that, although GA was initially put forth as a procedure to explain "economic growth" ex-post, it can similarly be used to plan "business growth" ex-ante when a general backward approach is taken in its procedure-called Backward Growth Accounting (BGA) in this paper. Taking this well-established economic-mathematical approach to planning business growth will enhance the current practices conceptually and structurally, as it is built on the basis of economic logic and mathematical tools. BGA can help businesses identify and plan for key drivers of output growth and assess shortcomings in the growth process, such as poor productivity, inadequate labor utilization, or insufficient capital investment. The paper outlines an eight-step procedure for planning business growth using BGA and includes appendices with real-world examples.C5, D2, L1, M11, M21, O4. This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited.

title: The Case Law of the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights in Libya Following the Arab Uprisings: Lessons Learned for the Consolidation and Legitimation of the Court

detail.title: The Case Law of the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights in Libya Following the Arab Uprisings: Lessons Learned for the Consolidation and Legitimation of the Court
detail.abstract: This article examines the two cases brought before the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights following the Libyan uprising in 2011: African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (Benghazi) v Libya and African Commission (Saif al-Islam Gaddafi) v Libya. These two cases mark three ‘firsts’: the first time for the African Commission to transfer a case to the African Court; the first order for provisional measures by the Court; and the first time the Court rendered a judgment by default. This study reveals that although the Court has taken significant steps in terms of its consolidation and legitimation, substantive and procedural challenges in its functioning remain. Moreover, the authors argue that the political divisions within the African Union diminished the Court’s potential impact on the Libyan crisis.

title: Shaming Climate Wrongdoers
affiliations: The Max Stern Yezreel Valley College and George Mason University - Center for Climate Change Communication

detail.title: Shaming Climate Wrongdoers
detail.abstract: Climate law, policy, and governance have grown substantially in recent years, yet these efforts have achieved only modest success. This article spotlights an underexplored complementary strategy in policy, governance, and legal domains: climate shaming--the use of public condemnation to encourage climate-responsible behaviour among governments, corporations, and their leaders. While shaming has been studied and applied as a regulatory and governance tool in other contexts, only a small but growing body of scholarship has begun to examine its potential in the climate arena. Drawing on multidisciplinary research from the social sciences, the humanities, and law, we review and map the main strands of this emerging literature to show the diverse forms and potential of shaming mechanisms, actors, and messages in the climate domain. Based on this analysis, we identify several gaps in the literature and practice of climate shaming, including explicit regulatory shaming, intergovernmental shaming, shaming of regulators by civil-society actors, and regulatory shaming of industry leaders. We propose expanding the conceptual framework of climate shaming to encompass these neglected dimensions, with the aim of encouraging further research as well as policy and governance experimentation in this evolving field.

detail.abstract: The twenty-first century has seen the hyper-commercialisation of sports. With hyper-commercialisation has come competition from actors both powerful and passionate for a share of the economic pie. This competition has sometimes escalated into conflict over legal and economic rights requiring judicial adjudication. This article explores the similarities and differences in the twenty-first century application of United States antitrust and Australian competition law to commercial sports. detail.title: Systemic Risk in Banking of Dollarization Economy
detail.abstract: This study proposes an index to measure systemic risk in Ecuador’s private financial institutions, using microdata between 2004 and 2023. The analysis focuses on 14 private banks and, in a second stage, incorporates 22 credit unions to provide a broader view of the financial sector. The research first builds a micro dataset with 12 monthly variables per institution. A dynamic factor model is then estimated to capture systemic risk, followed by a structural vector autoregression that links the proposed index with output and prices to evaluate the transmission of financial shocks to the real sector. The results show that the banking sector has generally maintained stability through the steady expansion of assets and equity. However, periods of economic distress such as the 2008–2009 global financial crisis and the 2020–2021 pandemic revealed its vulnerability to adverse shocks. The impulse response analysis indicates that systemic risk shocks generate high short-term volatility and inflationary pressures but converge to stability over time. These findings highlight the dynamic and recurrent nature of systemic risk, reinforcing the need for continuous monitoring of solvency, profitability, and efficiency, particularly in credit unions.

title: Testing the Level of Cluster Structures in Panel Data Models

detail.title: Testing the Level of Cluster Structures in Panel Data Models
detail.abstract: The cluster-robust variance estimator (CRVE) has become the standard practice for inference in panel data models. However, the selection of the appropriate clustering level is often based on heuristic rules or researcher discretion rather than formal statistical tests. This paper proposes a novel test based on the ratio of t-statistics under different cluster structures to determine the proper clustering level in linear panel regression models. This test is applicable to various panel data settings, including static or dynamic specifications, as well as short or long panels. It is also applicable to test one-way cluster versus two-way cluster. We derive the asymptotic properties of the proposed test under a panel framework with individual dimension N and time dimension T. To implement the test, we employ the wild cluster bootstrap method and establish the consistency of the bootstrap procedure. Simulation studies and empirical applications demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed test.

title: Core Properties of Cost Sharing Approaches to Local Public Good Provision
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst and University of Oregon - Department of Economics

detail.title: Core Properties of Cost Sharing Approaches to Local Public Good Provision
detail.abstract: Equivalence between cores and Walrasian equilibrium is a bedrock result in the theory of competitive markets, inspiring a search for analogous results in public good economies. In the literature on local public goods, there has been extensive research on how price-based approaches (e.g., Lindahl pricing) relate to the core. However, share-based approaches have received significantly less attention. In this paper, we analyze the relationship between the core and two share-based approaches, CvdN equilibrium and its precursor share equilibrium. While there are possibilities for core inclusion of share equilibrium, we find that there is no direct relationship between CvdN equilibrium and the traditional core concepts. We demonstrate that CvdN equilibrium exhibits equivalence with the coalition formation core, which is a core concept that fully incorporates the endogenous nature of jurisdictions in CvdN equilibrium. We analyze how different facets of the equilibrium concepts -- blocking conditions, conjectural variations, and possibilities for transfers between agents -- contribute to core results or lack thereof. Our finding of limited core relationships may appear to be a disadvantage for share-based approaches. However, our work clarifies how well-established core results within the price-based literature rely on ad hoc assumptions that are necessitated by the price system-assumptions that are entirely avoided under cost sharing.

title: Under Pressure: Sovereign Debt Challenges in a Warming World
affiliations: , Banque de France and Banque de France

detail.title: Under Pressure: Sovereign Debt Challenges in a Warming World
detail.abstract: Climate change is already imposing significant economic costs on advanced economies, with extreme weather events disrupting supply chains, damaging infrastructure, and straining public finances. Adaptation spending is increasing but remains insufficient to ensure long-term resilience. There is a trade-off between allowing climate damages to occur, which reduces economic growth and shrinks the fiscal base, or investing public funds in adaptation measures that reduce future damages but increase immediate fiscal costs. This paper explores this trade-off and compares it with mitigation strategies, which, while incurring short-term transition costs, can help reduce long-term economic and financial risks. The results underscore the need for a balanced approach, integrating both adaptation and mitigation efforts, to ensure economic stability and sustainable public debt over the long run.

title: Current Landscape of the Real-World Asset (RWA) Tokenization Ecosystem
affiliations: Donald G. Costello College of Business at George Mason University

detail.title: Current Landscape of the Real-World Asset (RWA) Tokenization Ecosystem
detail.abstract: The tokenization of real-world assets (RWAs) represents a pivotal development at the intersection of traditional financial markets and decentralized finance. This study undertakes a systematic examination of the RWA ecosystem through detailed due diligence of more than 180 products spanning six major asset classes: private credit, stocks, global bonds, commodities, institutional funds, and U.S. Treasuries. Our methodology combines a standardized review of legal structures and custodial arrangements with empirical analyses of on-chain transaction data. The analysis reveals that the RWA market, while still nascent, has already reached a scale exceeding $25 billion and exhibits strong concentration, with dominant platforms accounting for over 80% of market share in several segments. Tokenization has facilitated fractional ownership and contributed to the establishment of novel legal-technical frameworks, particularly Swiss-based special purpose vehicles (SPVs) and U.S.-based statutory trusts. However, the oft-cited promise of enhanced on-chain liquidity remains largely unfulfilled. Instead, the data reveal a persistent divergence between the theoretical advantages of 24/7 trading and the empirical reality of limited secondary-market activity and predominantly passive holding patterns. By providing a comprehensive survey of the current RWA landscape, this research identifies the structural frictions that must be addressed for the market to evolve from an experimental proof-of-concept into a mature, institutionally integrated asset class.

title: An Integral Equation Arising in the Analysis of Investment and Consumption with Stochastic Income

detail.abstract: We examine an integral equation arising in the analysis of investment and consumption with stochastic income. In particular, we revisit the integral equation from Bensoussan and Park (2025) and solve the equation numerically. We thoroughly discuss a priori estimates for the various functions of interest. We then develop a convenient and efficient numerical scheme for solving the integral equation via polynomial approximation and Guassian quadrature. We implement the numerical solution and investigate its sensitivity, generating some numerical results on the value function and the resulting optimal consumption and investment strategies with stochastic income.

title: The Benefits of Intentions: Deliberate Harm Avoidance and Consumer Responses
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and Financial Conduct Authority

detail.title: The Benefits of Intentions: Deliberate Harm Avoidance and Consumer Responses
detail.abstract: This paper investigates why firms engage in costly environmental and ethical practices, focusing on whether consumer responses depend on firms' intentions or outcomes. Existing literature links ESG practices to positive performance and stakeholder rewards, but most evidence is observational and cannot disentangle intentionality from outcomes. Using a controlled experiment, we examine consumer reactions when firms choose between a "clean" technology (avoiding harm at a cost) and a "dirty" technology (higher returns with negative externalities). Two treatments isolate intentionality: Random Choice versus Willful Choice. After observing the firm's choice and the resulting externality, consumers can respond by transferring (taking away) resources to the firm in a give-or-take Dictator Game. We find a pronounced asymmetry in how intentions matter. Consumers punish firms whenever a negative externality is incurred, regardless of intentionality, indicating that punitive responses are largely outcome-driven. By contrast, when harm is avoided, intentions play a central role: firms that deliberately choose to prevent a negative externality are treated with significantly greater leniency than firms for which absence of harm arises randomly, reflected in positive transfers on average. These findings highlight that intentionality affects punitive responses and helps explain why firms may voluntarily adopt costly ethical practices when choices are observable.

title: Infrastructure Development Issues in Regional Trade Agreements
affiliations: Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO)

detail.title: Infrastructure Development Issues in Regional Trade Agreements
detail.abstract: In the contemporary global economic paradigm, infrastructure has undergone a conceptual transformation, evolving from a basic facilitative prerequisite to a cornerstone strategic asset. Its quality and scope directly influence national competitive advantage and long-term developmental pathways. The establishment of sophisticated, integrated infrastructure systems operates as a principal catalyst, stimulating not only sustained economic growth but also measurable enhancements in societal well-being. Through the expansion of market access, reduction of transactional costs, and optimisation of resource distribution, such development underpins enduring progress. Infrastructure expenditure is characterised by a potent multiplier effect, engendering employment, augmenting fiscal revenues, and stimulating output within interconnected sectors. In a context defined by the realignment of global value chains and the search for novel economic drivers, transnational infrastructure projects have become indispensable. They extend advantages beyond domestic frontiers, reinforce regional economic cohesion, and actively reconfigure patterns of international commerce. Prevailing trade orthodoxy now unequivocally recognises that commercial volume and efficiency are contingent upon infrastructural capability to a degree comparable with the removal of tariff barriers. This realisation is particularly salient for emerging economies, where infrastructural shortfalls often constitute the most significant impediment to socio-economic development. Historically, the integration of infrastructure considerations within the framework of international trade governance was fragmented. A marked transition is now observable. The most recent cohort of Regional Trade Agreements (RTAs) reflects a heightened state commitment to formalising the critical interdependence between trade expansion and cooperative infrastructure planning. Scrutiny of contemporary accords reveals a continuum of approaches for institutionalising such collaboration. These legal instruments are progressively codifying distinct priorities—encompassing digitalised customs procedures, renewable energy grids, enhanced transport corridors, and resilient urban systems—thereby consolidating infrastructure as an indispensable element within the architecture of modern trade governance.

title: What if the Dollar Collapses?

detail.title: What if the Dollar Collapses?
detail.abstract: Dollar is a fiat paper currency and an international payment system since last 80 years or so. Since the founding of the US central bank Federal Reserve it has lost almost all of its purchasing power. Distrust in dollar is building among the BRICS nations who are rivals of the US in the great game of geopolitics. Sooner or later dollar will collapse. In this article I discuss likely consequences of US dollar collapse.

title: Overcoming Polarization through Simple Conciliatory Messages
affiliations: University of Oxford

detail.title: Overcoming Polarization through Simple Conciliatory Messages
detail.abstract: Political polarization has prevented cooperation and spurred hate and sometimes violence between political factions in the U.S. and other countries. Here I test experimentally whether two simple, conciliatory messages can improve relations between Democrats and Republicans in the U.S.: i) Acknowledging that the other side has good intentions and ii) sharing blame for hate and polarization. I find that subjects have better attitudes (in terms of altruism, trust, closeness perceptions, and openness to friendship) towards outgroup members who support one of the conciliatory messages than to outgroup members who don't, even though I hold outgroup members' policy views constant in the experimental design. However, subjects have worse attitudes towards ingroup members who support a conciliatory message than towards ingroup members who don't. I present evidence regarding potential mechanisms. Beliefs about how altruistic ingroup and outgroup members would behave towards the subject follow the same pattern as attitudes. Thus, the messages signal changes in benevolence. Outgroup members who support a message are perceived to be more benevolent and ingroup member who support a message are perceived to be less benevolent.

title: Harness Machine Learning with Carry
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) - School of Banking and Finance, Tsinghua University - PBC School of Finance and Tsinghua University - PBC School of Finance

detail.title: Harness Machine Learning with Carry
detail.abstract: We introduce a hybrid machine learning approach for predicting corporate bond returns that explicitly incorporates the structure of bond returns. Our method combines the model-free expected return from the yield curve (carry) with machine learning forecasts of the residual price return component. Using a comprehensive dataset of over 2.5 million U.S. bond-month observations, we show this hybrid framework significantly outperforms conventional machine learning that directly targets total returns, achieving higher out-of-sample predictive accuracy. While these forecasts generate economically meaningful gross returns in portfolio strategies, transaction costs substantially erode net performance. The profitability of machine learning signals is concentrated in periods of low market liquidity, suggesting they capture temporary, liquidity-driven mispricing more than persistent risk premia. Our results caution against direct application of equity-style ML to bonds and highlight the importance of incorporating fixed-income structure and trading frictions.

title: When History Rhymes: Reconstructing Hidden Geometry to Predict Irregular Cycles
affiliations: University of Edinburgh Business School and Monash University - Department of Econometrics & Business Statistics

detail.title: When History Rhymes: Reconstructing Hidden Geometry to Predict Irregular Cycles
detail.abstract: Irregular cycles are common in natural, engineered, and financial systems, yet their long-horizon prediction remains challenging because their dynamics do not recur in a consistent or periodic manner. Here we introduce the PillarScape Assembler (PiSA), a geometric reconstruction framework that recovers hidden structure directly from multivariate observations. Instead of fitting parametric models, PiSA rebuilds the system's evolving configuration in a fused phase space and identifies past trajectories whose geometry closely matches the present. This approach enables accurate long-range forecasts even in settings traditionally viewed as unpredictable. Across synthetic chaotic dynamics (Thomas attractor), astrophysical data (sunspot cycles), and climate variability (ENSO anomalies), PiSA consistently outperforms 27 state-ofthe-art statistical and machine-learning models. These findings show that reclaiming a system's latent geometric organization can substantially improve predictability in complex dynamical processes.

title: Liability For Damages Caused By Autonomous Driving Vehicles From The Eu Law Perspective
affiliations: University of Zagreb and University of Zagreb

detail.title: Liability For Damages Caused By Autonomous Driving Vehicles From The Eu Law Perspective
detail.abstract: The rise of autonomous driving vehicles and artificial intelligence systems presents significant legal challenges in various regulatory fields. Among them is main subject of this paper: liability for damages caused by autonomous driving vehicles. Common regulatory approach of liability caused by vehicles is based on fault or negligence. The legal subjects responsible for causing the accident are held liable for damages. Traditional liability legal frameworks, designed for human drivers, struggle to address the complexities introduced by vehicles operated with assistance of artificial intelligence. When it comes to artificial intelligence systems general regulatory approach varies from extensive risk-based framework best represented by the new European Union Artificial Intelligence Act to the liberal technology friendly approach like one adopted in the United States. Particular focus of this research is on the European Union Product Liability Directive. The new Directive plays a crucial role in holding manufacturers and software developers accountable with application of its rules on strict product liability. Paper explores its interconnection with Artificial Intelligence Act when it comes to liability for damages caused by autonomous driving vehicles. Other legislative efforts aiming to fill regulatory gaps and establish clear rules for liability of damages caused by autonomous driving vehicles are also explored. The interplay between existing and emerging European Union liability frameworks is elaborated. The paper detects the need for harmonized legal standards to ensure consumer protection, fair compensation mechanisms, and legal certainty in the context of accidents related to the use of autonomous driving vehicles.

title: Liquidity Fragility and Asymmetric Price Discovery in Crypto-Asset Markets: An Event-Based Microstructure Analysis

detail.title: Liquidity Fragility and Asymmetric Price Discovery in Crypto-Asset Markets: An Event-Based Microstructure Analysis

detail.abstract: This study investigates the relation between trade imbalance, volatility, and liquidity costs in the BTC/USDT market by utilizing high-frequency Level 2 (L2) tick data. Through implementation of an event-based aggregation framework (Clark, 1973; Lopez de Prado, 2018), we partition market activity into "eras" of 50,000 trades to normalize for intraday seasonality and non-linear information arrival. The empirical results indicate that net signed trade imbalance is a substantial driver of price discovery, therefore explaining 42.9% to 47.1% of price variance (R 2) across different scales. Furthermore, we identify a statistically significant widening of bid-ask spreads during high-volatility regimes, consistent with adverse selection models (Glosten & Milgrom, 1985). Finally, we provide exploratory evidence of structural asymmetry: at a 100,000-trade scale, the magnitude of sell-side price impact exceeds buy-side impact by $30.46. This downward fragility provides empirical support for the Financial Accelerator and Margin Spiral frameworks, suggesting that automated liquidations and risk-mitigation by market makers create a non-linear "loss spiral" unique to the digital asset microstructure.

title: Unintended Consequences of Employee Disclosure Mandates
affiliations: University at Buffalo (SUNY) - School of Management, Haas School of Business - UC Berkeley and University at Buffalo, SUNY

detail.title: Unintended Consequences of Employee Disclosure Mandates
detail.abstract: In 2021, California enacted Assembly Bill 701 (AB 701), the first U.S. regulation mandating warehouse employers to disclose productivity quotas to its employees. The law was designed to enhance workplace transparency and improve employee well-being by requiring employers to provide workers with detailed information about performance expectations and disciplinary consequences. We examine the real effects of this employee-level disclosure mandate on firm investment and employment outcomes. Using county-industry data from 2015-2024, we estimate difference-indifferences regressions comparing warehouse establishments in California to those in other U.S. counties. We find that warehouse facilities, employment, and total wage growth in California decline by approximately 8-9% relative to unaffected regions following AB 701's implementation. We find similar investment shifts when we employ related industries within California not covered by AB 701 as an alternative control group. Welfare analyses suggest that AB 701 resulted in additional negative effects in terms of shareholder returns and average employee pay. Our findings show that AB 701 produced unintended consequences by reducing instate investment and labor demand. We contribute to the literature on mandatory disclosure by highlighting how targeted transparency requirements, even when pro-social in intent, can shift firms' capital and labor allocation decisions across geographic boundaries.

title: Systems Thinking and Leadership Architecture: How Complexity, Purpose, and Behaviour Shape Executive Judgement

detail.title: Systems Thinking and Leadership Architecture: How Complexity, Purpose, and Behaviour Shape Executive Judgement

detail.abstract: Organisational failure is rarely sudden. It develops gradually beneath operational continuity, emerging only after the internal structure has already passed the point of recoverability. This paper positions complexity misinterpretation, not information scarcity, as the primary cause of institutional collapse. Its purpose is twofold: first, to advance leadership as an architectural discipline capable of pre-failure detection; and second, to introduce scientific and technical system tools through which leaders can interpret complexity structurally rather than behaviourally. It argues that resilience is lost during periods where output appears stable but decision architecture, capability density and response velocity are already in decline. Four core diagnostic models are presented. The Indexx(e) Systems Leadership Development Model™ defines a six-stage progression through Detect Complexity, Interpret Patterns, Architect Meaning, Select Behaviour, Time Decisions and Execute Judgement. The Decision Structure Model™ (DSM) explains how decisions originate, gate and layer within a system, forming compound load. The Organisational Decision Model™ (ODM) maps how decisions propagate across boundaries, revealing where distortion or acceleration materialises. The Stakeholder Mapping Framework identifies influence centres and interference vectors that shape executive judgement. Automotive case analysis is used to demonstrate deterioration mechanics in practice: Lotus illustrates capability erosion beneath visible performance; MINI shows strategic displacement despite retained manufacturing continuity; Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) reveals shock exposure where hidden fatigue becomes visible only under stress. This aligns with Porter's assertion that sustainable advantage is not derived from resources alone, but from an organisation's ability to interpret complexity and adapt at the rate of environmental change. Across cases, failure began privately and matured silently. The contribution of this work is an architecture for pre-failure detection, reframing leadership as a multi-layered scientific and technical discipline of interpretation, timing and systemic foresight rather than post-event reaction. It formalises DSM, ODM and Stakeholder Mapping as diagnostic tools and models capable of detecting deterioration before it becomes externally visible, positioning meaning-coherence, decision-flow integrity and systems-thinking capability as determinants of long-horizon performance and institutional continuity.

title: Does It Take Four to Tango in the Regulatory Competition for Global Listings? Comparing Regulations on Dual Class Shares among Singapore, Hong Kong, Mainland China, and Taiwan

detail.title: Does It Take Four to Tango in the Regulatory Competition for Global Listings? Comparing Regulations on Dual Class Shares among Singapore, Hong Kong, Mainland China, and Taiwan

publicationDetails.detailsText: Northwestern Journal of International Law & Business, Vol. 45, Issue 3, Pp. 283-327, 2025

detail.abstract: We provide a comparative analysis of regulatory competition among Singapore, Hong Kong, Mainland China, and Taiwan regarding the process, purpose, and actual results of deregulating Dual-Class Share (“DCS”) structure. The comparative analysis focuses on the role of regulatory competition in the convergence or divergence of DCS-structure regulations. To attract unicorn companies and China Concept Stock (“CCS”) companies to choose public offerings in regional exchanges, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Mainland China sequentially announced their amendments to listing rules, particularly in 2018, to allow public offerings of DCS-structure companies while considering their preference for the ownership structure of unicorns. We employ theories of regulatory competition and convergence to analyze the regulatory trajectories of the four jurisdictions in the Asia-Pacific region and how such jurisdictional competition would accelerate the transplantation of corporate governance regulations and, therefore, converge with the US permissive model in appearance. Hong Kong, Singapore, and Mainland China have transplanted the DCS-structure listing regulatory framework and added shareholder protection, particular disclosure, and sunset restrictions, which converge more in concert with each other towards the US model. We also discuss why and how stubborn path dependence would bring non-convergence towards the US model for listing companies in Taiwan, which is an outlier of the regulatory competition for global listings. By analyzing this competition by supplying DCS legal products among the four jurisdictions, we enrich the regulatory competition theory and study how this competition produces formal convergence and functional divergence of DCS structures in corporate governance regulations. We contribute to the existing literature by providing a comparative view of regulatory competition among the four jurisdictions and examining the potential impact of the US-China trade war on the deregulation of the DCS structure in the Asia-Pacific region.

title: Impact of Inventory on Production Smoothening in FMCG Supply Chain
affiliations: , Vivekananda Institute of Professional Studies- Technical Campus, University of Delhi and IIM Jammu

detail.title: Impact of Inventory on Production Smoothening in FMCG Supply Chain
detail.abstract: The FMCG sector is the cornerstone of any economy with significant contribution to GDP, employment and economic growth. The study aims to explore the relationship among production, demand, inventories and profit before interest and tax for FMCG sector in context of India. For analysis a panel data is employed with 64 firms of Indian FMGC sector, over 10-year time span from 2013-2023. To analyze cost structures and production, ordinary least square (OLS), fixed effect model and random effect model is utilized. It is found that demand, inventories and profit before interest and tax significantly impact Production. Furthermore, higher profitability helps firms to minimize their cost of production and operational costs. The study also highlights the unobserved heterogeneity across firms after employing Breusch-Pagan and Hausman test, illustrating variations in production techniques due to firm specific policies and strategies. Moreover, the inventories plays a significant role in production smoothening.

title: Fixing What We Didn't Break: Black Women, Racialized Labor, and Organizational Harm as a Determinant of Health

detail.title: Fixing What We Didn't Break: Black Women, Racialized Labor, and Organizational Harm as a Determinant of Health

detail.abstract:
Black women have long sustained equity work across institutions, yet the organizational
cultures they serve often extract their labor while remaining indifferent—or actively hostile—to
their well-being. This paper examines organizational culture as a determinant of health and a site
of racialized labor, arguing that the emotional, strategic, and psychological burdens
disproportionately placed on Black women are not incidental but structurally embedded.
Drawing from Black feminist theory, organizational studies, and public health literature, this
analysis critiques symbolic inclusion efforts and the weaponization of resilience, highlighting
how these dynamics undermine institutional credibility and the integrity of equity work itself.
Rather than prescribing surface-level reforms, the paper offers a reparative framework for
cultural transformation—centered on care, accountability, and power redistribution. It calls for a
shift from rhetorical commitments to structural change, insisting that equity must be
operationalized in ways that protect rather than exploit the people most critical to its success.

title: Infrastructure-Induced Welfare Costs in Electric Vehicle Charging Networks: A Stochastic Impulse Control Approach
affiliations: Corvinus University of Budapest and The University of Manchester

detail.title: Infrastructure-Induced Welfare Costs in Electric Vehicle Charging Networks: A Stochastic Impulse Control Approach
detail.abstract: This paper quantifies the long-run welfare costs imposed on electric vehicle users by limited accessibility and congestion in the public charging network. We develop a dynamic model of charging behavior in which drivers face a recurring trade-off between continuing their journey under uncertain charging availability and incurring the time and detour costs of recharging. Charging accessibility is summarized by an effective distance index that captures the spatial distribution of charging stations and its variability across road networks.The model delivers a region-specific, annualized measure of infrastructure-induced generalized cost, reflecting detours, queuing delays, breakdown risk, and range anxiety attributable solely to charging infrastructure limitations. We calibrate the model using detailed road-network and public charging-station data for Great Britain and apply it consistently across all regions.The results reveal pronounced spatial inequality in charging infrastructure adequacy. Infrastructure-induced welfare costs are several times higher in sparsely served regions such as Scotland than in dense urban areas such as London, even for identical users. Counterfactual experiments indicate that welfare outcomes are primarily driven by time-related frictions—particularly queuing delays and detour distances—while charging prices and breakdown penalties play a secondary role.The framework provides a tractable and empirically grounded tool for evaluating the adequacy of public charging infrastructure and for assessing the welfare implications of targeted network investments from a transportation planning perspective.

title: Network Stability under Monitoring
affiliations: Stanford University, Department of Economics, Stanford University and Stanford University

detail.title: Network Stability under Monitoring
detail.abstract: We study the stability of social networks when agents can monitor the linking decisions of others. A network is said to be Peer-Monitored Stable if any unilateral deletion or mutual addition of a link harms at least one neighboring agent. We show that, under two widely studied payoff structures-distance-based and degree-based-every Pareto-Efficient network is Peer-Monitored Stable. We then generalize the model by allowing agents to monitor indirect connections within a given distance, introducing a measure of network stability defined by the minimal monitoring radius required to stabilize a network. Finally, we apply this measure to mixed externalities models and derive non-trivial upper bounds on the monitoring radius needed to ensure the stability of Pareto-efficient networks under degree-distance-based payoffs

title: A Two-layer Multi-objective Planner for Heterogeneous UAV-assisted Rescue Considering Time-sensitive Demands and User Satisfaction
affiliations: Zhongyuan University of Technology, Zhongyuan University of Technology, Zhongyuan University of Technology, Zhongyuan University of Technology, Zhongyuan University of Technology, Zhongyuan University of Technology and Qatar University

detail.title: A Two-layer Multi-objective Planner for Heterogeneous UAV-assisted Rescue Considering Time-sensitive Demands and User Satisfaction
detail.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have been widely applied in many fields. In the mountainous disaster, user demand is dynamic in relation to the rescue processing. Additionally, the rescue priority is multi-parameter, and the UAV is heterogeneous. These facts bring the challenge of optimizing the efficiency and quality of rescuing. In this work, the heterogeneous multi-UAV rescue problem has been modeled, considering the UAV heterogeneity, the time-sensitive demands, and the regional diversity. On the UAV side, an energy-efficiency model has been constructed to minimize the total time consumption; on the user side, a rescue-quality model has been formulated to maximize the satisfaction level. The two-layer multi-objective planner has been developed. On the upper layer, a priority-aware clustering algorithm has been designed for task allocation in the dynamic scheduling; on the lower layer, a leader-guided NSGA-II (LGNSGA-II) has been designed to enhance convergence and solution diversity, integrating the Sobol-based initialized strategy, the dynamic adaptive crossover strategy, and the multi-leader directional mutation. The Sobol-based initialization strategy has been adopted to improve the diversity; the dynamic adaptive crossover strategy has been introduced to balance the exploration and local exploitation; the multi-leader directional mutation has been used to improve the adaptability. The experiments with three scenarios, including the 25, 50, and 100 disaster regions, have been executed to confirm the two-layer multi-objective planner. Some typical algorithms have been adopted for comparing the convergence speed and the Pareto quality. It has been found that the two-layer multi-objective planner can improve the efficiency and quality in heterogeneous UAV-assisted rescuing.

title: The Promise and Perils of Sustainable Supply Chain Finance
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School, Hong Kong Polytechnic University - Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies, University of Connecticut - Department of Operations & Information Management and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School

detail.title: The Promise and Perils of Sustainable Supply Chain Finance
detail.abstract: Firms increasingly deploy sustainable supply chain finance (sustainable SCF) to address two persistent frictions in responsible sourcing: upstream liquidity constraints and limited verifiability of sustainability performance. Although tying favorable payment terms to verified compliance is often viewed as a straightforward way to improve sustainability, the incentive effects depend critically on how early settlement interacts with verification credibility and downstream exposure when noncompliance is later uncovered. We develop a game-theoretic model of a retailer and a capital-constrained supplier to study sustainable SCF under internal versus third-party auditing. Three insights emerge. First, sustainable SCF does not mechanically increase compliance. By conditioning early payment on passing an audit, it creates heterogeneous incentives across supplier liquidity profiles and can sustain a partial-compliance equilibrium in which only the liquidity-urgent supplier type complies. Second, early settlement trades off relaxing supplier liquidity exposure against increasing the retailer's financing burden. As a result, sustainable SCF can either strengthen or weaken equilibrium sustainability, and it can generate win-win or lose-lose outcomes, depending on diversion opportunities for noncompliant goods as summarized by the supplier's secondary-market salvage value. Third, third-party auditing is not uniformly beneficial. While it may improve verification, it can also weaken compliance incentives if governance arrangements attenuate the retailer's effective exposure to greenwashing, reducing the retailer's willingness to pay for strict compliance when early settlement is costly. Overall, the results caution that sustainable SCF must be designed as an integrated system of payment timing, verification, and accountability, rather than as a standalone financing intervention.

title: Synthetic but Not Infinite: How Much LLM-Generated Data to use in Market Research
affiliations: and Cornell University - School of Operations Research and Information Engineering

detail.title: Synthetic but Not Infinite: How Much LLM-Generated Data to use in Market Research
detail.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed data generation by enabling scalable synthetic data augmentation. This paper studies a fundamental question in market research in the ago of generative AI: how much synthetic data should be used? In the existing literature, the proportion of LLM-generated synthetic data is usually treated as a hyperparameter, tuned by ad hoc experimentation. In addition, a more important yet unexplored question is how the optimal amount of synthetic data should vary across different population segments, e.g., between younger and older respondents.
In this work, we address these challenges by deriving a closed-form expression for this highly heterogeneous hyperparameter vector that governs the proportion of synthetic data. This prescriptive characterization arises from our analysis of a logit choice model that integrates real and synthetic data, under which we establish a finite-sample complexity bound for the estimation error of the resulting hybrid estimator. Specifically, our expression for the heterogeneous proportion of synthetic data corresponds to the one that minimizes this upper bound. We further demonstrate the strong empirical performance of our closed-form expression using both synthetic data and a real-world vaccine preference dataset. Overall, our results suggest that the closed-form expression serves as a practical and reliable empirical rule of thumb for determining how much LLM-generated synthetic data to incorporate into market research studies.

detail.abstract: The dynamic and volatile nature of financial markets requires decision tools that combine accurate stock movement forecasts with optimal portfolios derived from formulations that incorporate real-world trading constraints. This paper presents an integer-valued portfolio optimization framework that integrates next-day stock closing price predictions from machine learning (ML) models (XGBoost) into several Markowitz-type formulations. We evaluate multiple formulations including diversification constraints, explicit short-selling models (standard and volatilitynormalized / "Black-Scholes"-style), a Meta-Markowitz ensemble that hedges strategic risk across portfolios themselves, and a robust optimization variant under box uncertainty. Experiments on the Indian SENSEX constituent stocks (2010-2024 training window) show that MLinformed integer portfolios outperform the SENSEX and Markowitz-without-ML benchmarks with respect to five portfolio performance metrics including the Sharpe and Sortino ratios, while robust and meta strategies reduce downside risk. These experiments involve a comprehensive statistical analysis pipeline: Ljung-Box and augmented Dickey-Fuller tests for autocorrelation and stationarity prior to statistical comparison; Shapiro-Wilk tests of normality to determine whether nonparametric or parametric comparisons must be performed; and finally, a variety of parametric (Student's) and nonparametric (Friedman, Wilcoxon signed-rank) tests to assess performance of each Ml-informed portfolio against the benchmarks.

detail.abstract: Affirmative Vision: The Legal Defense Fund (LDF) envisions a future in which all people, especially Black people, have access to high-quality, racially integrated educational opportunities, from preschool through higher education. In pursuit of this mission, LDF advocates for the fair distribution of opportunities and resources, including preparation for college and careers, access to diverse and high-quality teachers, improved school facilities, and safe and supportive school environments. Black and non-Black students alike deserve an intellectually challenging, historically accurate, and culturally inclusive education that embraces the history, perspectives, and experiences of all groups. To achieve this goal, public schools must be funded equitably and equipped to meet the individual needs of all students, so that every student receives a quality education regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, disability status, immigration status, religion, color, national origin, or other social characteristics.  LDF relentlessly challenges laws and policies that seek to exclude the history, perspectives, and experiences of Black people and other historically marginalized communities from school activities and curricula. LDF uses legal advocacy, community organizing, social science research, storytelling, and policy reform to work toward a public education system that is inclusive, safe, and gives everyone equal access to high-quality academic instruction and school-based programming, while protecting against privatization, censorship, and attacks on civil rights. Education is a right and something that benefits everyone, so every person and every level of government must work together to ensure that all students in the United States have access to a free, high-quality public education. The first part of this paper explains the current state of the education system, which is marked by underfunded and segregated schools, disciplinary practices that target Black students, inequities in academic tracking, a lack of Black educators, and whitewashed curricula. The second part proposes policies to help Black people thrive by advancing school integration and funding equity, combating the attacks on truth in education, recruiting and retaining Black educators, ending exclusionary discipline and policing in schools, and defending the Department of Education.

detail.abstract: In this research, the costs of rare earth elements (REEs) due to the oligopolistic market structure are estimated. On the supply side, China exercises a dominant position in the international REEs market because it controls more than 40 percent of deposits and more than 60 percent of REEs traded. Other countries assume an ancillary role in international markets for these minerals, which will increasingly play a crucial role in economic growth in the coming decades, since REEs are considered the minerals of technology and the green transition. Using the fringe oligopoly model, the costs due to this market structure for economies less endowed with deposits of these minerals are estimated. To perform this analysis, the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index was calculated, and a new index of dependence on REEs, as a proxy for a country's economic vulnerability, was constructed. Our database covers fifty years and sixty-two countries. Most of the data used comes from the World Bank database. Using quantile econometric models, we can calculate the economic costs of countries with fewer REEs caused by the market power exerted by the leading country in this market and estimate the loss for each country involved in the international trade of these minerals. Finally, technological advancements play a pivotal role in aiding countries reliant on REEs to lower their costs. This can be achieved through policies aimed at minimizing the utilization of REEs during manufacturing, harnessing the recycling of minerals from used products, and discovering alternative materials to replace REEs.

detail.abstract: Food insecurity is a multidimensional and unobservable construct that is commonly assessed using a set of partially overlapping indicators. Using data from the 2023 Afghanistan Agriculture and Food Security Monitoring System survey, this paper examines the latent structure underlying commonly used food security measures, including food consumption, dietary diversity, food-based coping, and household hunger-based indicators. Exploratory factor analysis applied at the item level reveals that these measures capture multiple distinct dimensions of food insecurity rather than a single continuum, with substantial heterogeneity also observed within indicators. Relating extracted latent factors to existing composite measures highlights important implications for indicator selection, triangulation, and targeting in food security monitoring and humanitarian response.

title: The GENIUS Act's "Interest" Prohibition: Evidence of Regulatory Arbitrage in Digital Asset Markets

detail.title: The GENIUS Act's "Interest" Prohibition: Evidence of Regulatory Arbitrage in Digital Asset Markets
detail.abstract: This paper provides empirical evidence that the interest prohibition contained in the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act has been effectively circumvented through intermediated distribution structures. Using archival data from January 2024 through January 2026, I demonstrate that USDC "rewards" distributed through Coinbase exhibit a 98.7% correlation with 3-month Treasury Bill yields, with 95.6% pass-through efficiency and a stable 21-basis-point intermediation spread. Ordinary least squares regression analysis with a structural break variable reveals that the Act's July 2025 enactment produced no statistically significant decoupling effect. These findings suggest that the statutory prohibition on "interest or yield" payments has been rendered ineffective through relabeling and structural intermediation. The economic substance of these rewards may trigger scrutiny under the Howey and Reves tests, potentially classifying them as securities despite their nomenclature. This research demonstrates the limitations of prohibition-based regulatory approaches in digital asset markets, a conclusion reinforced by Coinbase's successful January 2026 intervention to block similar interest prohibition language in the proposed Digital Asset Market Clarity Act of 2025 (Clarity).

The paper proposes a restructured MSP framework built on income insurance, combining limited cereal procurement,

detail.abstract: This study offers a comprehensive and comparative analysis of digital diplomacy as a transformative force reshaping states' soft power in the 21st century. Building on classical and contemporary theories of power, public diplomacy, and strategic communication, the article examines how digital platforms, algorithms, and networked publics reconfigure attraction, legitimacy, and influence. Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative, comparative casestudy design drawing on document analysis, digital content analysis, and thematic coding. The article advances the concept of "digital soft power" to capture these dynamics and offers policy implications for strategic communication, institutional coordination, capacity-building, and ethical governance. By integrating theory with extensive case evidence, the study contributes to debates on power in the digital age and provides a framework for understanding influence in platformized international relations.

detail.abstract: This paper reconstructs and critically evaluates John Rawls's argument that social and economic inequalities are justifiable only when they arise within a scheme of fair cooperation among free and equal persons. Focusing on Rawls's rejection of desert-based justifications for inequality, the paper examines how the original position and the veil of ignorance function to exclude morally arbitrary advantages from the justification of political principles. Rawls's two principles of justice are interpreted not as distributive rules grounded in merit or efficiency, but as institutional constraints designed to secure reciprocity and public legitimacy. The analysis argues that Rawls offers a compelling account of why natural talents and social starting points cannot ground moral entitlement to greater reward, and why inequalities must be justified to those who are least advantaged. At the same time, the paper critically assesses persistent objections concerning effort, responsibility, motivation, and the limits of ideal theory. While Rawls's framework faces challenges in accounting for intuitions about individual responsibility and in addressing non-ideal conditions of structural injustice, the paper contends that these difficulties do not undermine his core insight. Justice as fairness is best understood as a normative standard for evaluating the moral legitimacy of social institutions rather than as a comprehensive theory of personal desert. By situating distributive justice within the context of social cooperation and institutional design, the paper defends Rawls's approach as a powerful alternative to moralized and entitlement-based accounts of inequality.

title: Entitlement, Redistribution, and the Limits of Patterned Justice in Robert Nozick

detail.abstract: This paper reconstructs and critically evaluates Robert Nozick's entitlement theory of justice as presented in Anarchy, State, and Utopia. Rejecting patterned and end-state principles of distribution, Nozick argues that justice in holdings depends exclusively on historical processes of just acquisition and voluntary transfer. Through his critique of patterned principles and his defense of self-ownership, Nozick contends that redistributive taxation beyond the minimal functions of the state constitutes an unjust form of coercion analogous to forced labor. The paper argues that Nozick's entitlement theory offers a powerful and morally illuminating defense of individual liberty and voluntary exchange, successfully exposing the tension between liberty and distributive patterns. At the same time, it contends that the theory relies on idealized assumptions about historical acquisition, background justice, and social cooperation that limit its plausibility in non-ideal conditions. The paper concludes that while Nozick provides a stringent constraint on state action and a compelling critique of redistribution, his entitlement theory falls short as a comprehensive account of distributive justice in societies shaped by structural inequality and historical injustice.

title: The Efficiency-Fragility Limit: Slack, Volatility, and Collapse Boundaries in Complex Systems
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Efficiency-Fragility Limit: Slack, Volatility, and Collapse Boundaries in Complex Systems
detail.abstract: Efficiency is typically optimized on mean performance. Fragility, however, is paid in tails: rare delays, long recovery times, and discontinuous collapse under volatility. This paper states and motivates an Efficiency-Fragility Limit (EFL): for a broad class of systems that must process stochastic load with finite capacity, reducing slack yields approximately linear gains in average utilization but superlinear growth in delay, variance, and tail risk as utilization approaches one. The result is not a moral claim about "waste," but a structural constraint: zeroslack operation is generically unstable outside of near-deterministic environments. We anchor the EFL in three canonical domains-queueing, inventory, and feedback control-and connect it to empirical early-warning signatures such as critical slowing down and thickening delay tails. We then sketch how the same geometry appears in software delivery, large-scale computing, biological reserve capacity, and hospital operations. Finally, we define falsifiers and measurement guidance for diagnosing when "efficiency programs" are actually boundary-shifts that export fragility to enclosing systems.

detail.abstract: This paper attempts to mathematically define the function of the "organization" (firm), which is often abstracted in neoclassical general equilibrium theory, through a reinterpretation of the identity of Walras' Law. Conventional theories, such as Human Capital Theory (Becker) and the Rational Expectations Hypothesis (Lucas), have attributed disequilibria and rigidities in the labor market to individual skill characteristics or informational imperfections (illusions) on the part of agents. In contrast, this paper introduces an equilibrium condition derived by transforming Walras' Law. We define an organization as a "structural buffer mechanism" that absorbs excess demand in the goods market (negative shock) by equating it with excess supply in the labor market (internal surplus). From this perspective, we demonstrate that business cycles and employment practices can be explained not as market failures or agent errors, but as structural necessities for the survival of organizations within a market economy.

detail.abstract: This paper examines product mix optimization when unit costs depend on production volumes. Traditional approaches assume costs are fixed, yet in practice overhead allocations vary with total output and raw material prices often change with procurement scale. These dependencies create feedback loops between volumes and costs that can alter the optimal allocation of capacity and affect projected profitability. An iterative linear and mixed-integer optimization framework with endogenous cost feedback is developed in which production volumes are optimized subject to capacity and product-level bounds, costs are recalculated to reflect the resulting mix, and the process is repeated until stability is reached. The approach demonstrates how incorporating feedback effects yields production plans that are operationally feasible and more consistent with income statement forecasts.

title: Do Leadership Transitions Degrade Law Enforcement? Evidence from Sheriff Elections

detail.title: Do Leadership Transitions Degrade Law Enforcement? Evidence from Sheriff Elections
detail.abstract: How disruptive are leadership changes in local law enforcement? While a large body of literature studies the performance effects of electoral turnover among local officials, little is known about county sheriffs. Sheriff elections generate abrupt leadership changes in agencies with substantial authority, raising questions about whether turnover disrupts operations or whether institutional continuity mitigates such effects. This paper investigates whether electoral turnover in law enforcement impacts arrest rates. Using hand-collected data on sheriff elections merged with arrest records, I employ a difference-indifferences design to examine how arrest rates respond, first, to an incumbent sheriff's electoral defeat and, second, to the subsequent transition to new leadership. I find that election losses lead to modest declines in arrests for lower-level offenses, while no significant effects are observed for arrest rates of severe offenses. In contrast, the transition to a new sheriff shows little impact on arrest activity. Analysis of deputy employment data suggests that staffing declines may drive the decrease in arrests following election losses.

title: South Africa: Populism's Next Target

detail.title: South Africa: Populism's Next Target
detail.abstract: Following news of Jacob Zuma's resignation from office, Jessie Duarte, the Deputy Secretary General of the African National Congress (ANC) party, struck a tone that was more elegiac, rather than energetic about the former president's departure. During a press briefing immediately after Zuma's speech, Duarte noted that the ANC's "decision to impose a recall was taken only after exhaustive discussions," lauding Zuma as a "disciplined member" of the ANC. That the decision to remove Zuma, whose epoch is best characterized by economic mismanagement, rampant unemployment, increased crime, and corruption took so long spells trouble for the ANC. Cyril Ramaphosa, who succeeded Zuma as the president of the ANC in December and will take over the reins from Zuma once more in the office of the presidency, inherits a nation that has seen the erosion of its democratic institutions and has slipped into irrelevance among the world's notable emerging economies. Furthermore, as the only majority party in power during the youthful history of South Africa's democracy, the ANC has seen its brand blemished by recalls that took down Zuma and his predecessor, Thabo Mbeki.
